translations.text: [A work] of our holy and God-clad father Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, brother of the holy and great Basil, [on] what was lacking in the description of the Six Days, which the blessed and great Basil set forth earlier; and since the [account of the] creation of man was left unfinished by him,
this the holy Gregory completed, loftily and in a manner glorified by God. To my brother and servant of God, Peter the bishop, Gregory, bishop of Nyssa. Bless us, father!
If it were proper to honor those distinguished in virtue with the honor of possessions and goods, as Solomon says,

the possessions of the whole world would not be worthy to be set against your virtues, but would be paltry and beyond comparison with them. But since the grace due to your honor is higher than the value of all riches, and the holy Fullness exacts from us the gift of love according to custom,
we send this kind of gift to your holiness, O man of God: an offering small and not equal to your worth, yet not falling short of our ability.
This gift is a discourse, like some paltry garment, woven not without difficulty by this poor mind of ours.
The subject of this discourse may perhaps appear presumptuous to many, yet let it not be reckoned as going beyond what is proper,
for the creatures of God were duly examined by him alone who was truly created in the image of God, and who beautified and adorned his soul with the likeness of God: our common father and teacher,
who, through his understanding, made the sublime order of all created things something all could contemplate and examine.
And the world, created by the true wisdom of God, he made known and plain to the newly instructed through the understanding of his wisdom.
But we, although we fall short of being worthy of admiring him, have set our hearts on completing what was lacking in that great man's examination,
not so as to spoil his great labors by the paltriness of what we say, or to add some superior understanding (for how could it be right for that lofty voice to be insulted by our useless words!),
but so that it may not be supposed that the honor of the teacher is held of little account among his disciples. For

if none of his disciples had set his heart on completing what remained, the creation of man that was lacking from the "Six Days," perhaps some stain would have touched his great glory, as though he had not thought it proper, nor wished, to plant any pattern of understanding among those who listened to and obeyed his words and teachings.
But now, since we have ventured, according to our ability, to relate what was left remaining, if anything of this kind should be found among our words

that is not unworthy of his teaching, let the grace and cause of it be reckoned without doubt to the teacher. But if it fails to reach the understanding of that all-wise man, the great man will stand above the charge we mentioned earlier, that he did not wish to advance anything right and desirable among his disciples, and we shall rightly be blamed by accusers, as those who, through the smallness of our hearts, were unable to receive the wisdom of the teacher.

But this subject that lies before us is not small, nor of little account for consideration, nor inferior to the great wonders of the creation of the world; perhaps it is even greater than all the things of creation, for among created things nothing that exists has been made like the Creator except man alone.
Therefore it will not be hard for understanding hearers to pardon us for what has been said here, even if our discourse falls far short of the worth of the subject.

For, as I think, one who treats this subject must deal with what concerns all men: those who were first created, those who are now alive, and those who are to come hereafter, so that nothing may be left uninvestigated.

And if this is not done, the zeal of our undertaking would surely be convicted of deficiency, if anything is lacking in the account of the making of man, which is set before us for examination, or if any of the things that are fitting is passed over,
but also that which may even be thought contrary with regard to him, because it was not seen in him from the beginning among those first created,

and now, out of some necessary compulsion, has come to be seen in his nature; it is incumbent on us, by the interpretation and teaching of the Scriptures and by the discovery of reasonings, to soften and harmonize it,

so that everything may be fitted together and one thing reconciled with another, through the joining and harmonizing of those things thought to be opposed, so that they may arrive at one perfection; and may this be done through hope in the divine power, which is the hope of the hopeless and the helper of the helpless.

And for the sake of understanding and clarity, I have thought it fitting to write out the readings chapter by chapter, so that it may be easy for you to know from the very beginning, through a few words,
the force and teaching of all that follows, through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 1,

in which there is some natural philosophy concerning the world and a brief account of the things created before the making of man. This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, as the divine Scripture says,

when all these visible things had been finished and made complete, and each of the things that exist had been separated and set apart in its own structure, when the body of the heavens had encompassed all visible things,
and earth and water, heavy and downward-flowing matter, occupied the middle place of all things, holding each other firm and united with one another.
And the bond and stability of creation was given to the nature of existing things by the divine craftsmanship and power, which guides all things by the yoke of twofold aids and activities,

for by rest and motion it ordained and established the bringing of non-existent things into being and the standing and enduring of existing things; for upon that heavy, unchanging and motionless nature,
as upon some firm axle, it arranged this rapid and swift revolution of the heaven, in the manner of a cart wheel,

which revolves upon that axle of stability; and through each other it keeps both of them indissoluble, for by the rapid revolution of the circling nature it encompasses the dense matter of the earth and compresses it,
and so that firm and motionless [?] element, by its unmoved stability, unceasingly strengthens the motion and revolution of the things revolving around it.
Now between the two of them, things separated from each other, there arises an equal extreme of qualities: the stationary nature and the unresting constitution,
for neither does the earth change from its firmness, nor does the heaven ever slacken from its great and swift motion.
And these, as the first and chief of beings, were created by the wisdom of the Creator before all other beings, as the foundations of all material things. And, as I think,
the great Moses for this reason sets forth the creation of heaven and earth by God first: to show that all these visible created things came into being, by the divine will, from motion and rest.
That is to say, heaven and earth, separated from each other equally by opposing qualities,

share with each other through the parts established between them, and of themselves become mediators for those parts. And so that the union of opposites with each other through intermediaries may be made clear, understand it in this way:
Air resembles the ever-moving and subtle nature of fire through the lightness of its nature and its perpetual motion,
and yet it does not become foreign to kinship with the firm elements. It neither stands forever motionless, nor again does it wholly flow away and disperse,
but by a property of a twofold kind it becomes a boundary between the opposing things,

for by itself it at once unites and divides those things that are separated by nature. And in the same way the moist nature too, through twofold richnesses [?] and conditions, is joined in a double and two-sided manner to the opposites,
for through its heaviness and downward course it has great kinship with the earth, while through its going and flowing it is not foreign to the moving natures,
but it is a uniter and gatherer of those things that are in conflict,

for it changes heaviness into motion, and through heaviness it is not held back from motion. And thus those things far separated from each other by nature are united, having come into unity through the intermediaries. And if one is to speak truly,
not even the natures of the opposites are wholly without a share in one another and foreign to each other in kinship and property,
and thus all the material things of the world look toward each other and share with one another, even through their distinct and separate constitutions,
for motion is seen not only in change from place to place, but it also appears in alteration and turning.
And again, likewise, the motionless nature does not have the motion of displacement, yet through decay and renewal it moves and changes perpetually,
for the wisdom of God arranged this exchange of properties in such a way that it gave unchangeableness to what is ever moving, and assigned alteration to what is motionless.

And by a certain boundless providence he arranged this, so that when that natural property, which is motionlessness and unchangeableness, is seen in these visible constitutions, created things should not come to be thought of as gods, for motion and change are inaccessible to and foreign from the divine nature. And where these are seen, there the suspicion of divinity no longer enters.

For this reason the earth is firmly established and yet not unchanging, whereas heaven, conversely, has no change, but neither does it have stability, that is, immobility; for to the stationary nature [the divine power assigned] change,

and to the unchanging nature the divine power assigned motion as its own, and thus it allotted to the two of them properties exchanged with one another, and made them foreign to any suspicion of divinity,
for neither of these is attributed to the divine nature, neither instability nor change, as we said above.
Thus, then, everything was completed in its own constitution and attained its own measure. And heaven and earth and all the things between them were finished in the making, as Moses said,
and each of them was adorned with a fitting beauty. For heaven shone with the light of the luminaries,

and the sea and the air were adorned by the swimming creatures and the birds of the air, and the earth by the variety of all plants and four-footed animals, all of which, empowered by the divine will, it brought forth and bore all together in an instant.
And thus the earth was adorned with beauty, and together with the flowers it put forth fruits, and the gardens were full of the plants

that befit gardens, and all the mountains and hills and mountain peaks and sunny slopes and flatlands and plains, and all the newly blossoming green growth in the gullies and ravines, and all the woodlands [?] and groves were crowned with the adornment of trees of various kinds,

which had only then sprung up from the earth and in an instant grew to the fullness of perfect beauty, and all of them rejoiced and were glad and frolicked at the command of God. The livestock, brought to life in herds and droves, set apart and according to their several kinds, both rested and ran about in the mountains and hills and all the groves,
and all the open lands and groves resounded with the merriment and singing of the birds.

And again, in the same way, the expanse of the sea, its appearance and its beauty, gave a further loveliness, and, having only now come to rest in calm and stillness and been gathered into its gathering-place, it was delightful to behold,

and its refuges and anchorages and harbors, cut out of their own accord by the divine will among the cliffs and rocks, calmed it and joined to the dry land [?] and the earth the softness of the sea; and again those delightful ripples [?] and gently released murmurs were adorned with the beauty of the havens,
and the faint breezes and light airs, with the quiet blowing of winds over the face of the sea, made those shining waves, stirred up with a smile, blossom.
And all the wealth of sea and dry land and the adornment of all created things stood ready.

Chapter 2. And why was man created last, after all the creatures? Because there was as yet no one who could make use of and rejoice in the things that had been made; for man, this great and honorable creature,

had not yet been created, nor had he entered among those beings created earlier, for it was not fitting that the ruler should appear before those over whom he was to have rule; rather, it was fitting that the realm be prepared first, and only then that the king be brought in.
But since the Creator of all, as royal courts,

Thus he prepared for the one who was to be king the sea and the dry land, heaven and earth, the groves and the rivers, and he bent this all-beautiful world over them like a roof and a vault, and in these royal places he stored up wealth of every kind.
And by wealth I mean all created things, as many as are seen among trees and plants, and as many as are among creatures that have sense, breath and life;
and if material things too ought to be counted as wealth, all those that for their color and brilliance are held precious in the eyes of men, such as gold and silver and these gems and carbuncles,
which men love, the abundance of all these he hid in the bosom of the earth, as if in royal treasuries of some kind,
and only then did he bring man forth into the world, to be a beholder of some of his wonders and lord of others, so that through his enjoyment he might have understanding of the Giver,
and give thanks, and through the beauty and greatness of created things search out the inexpressible and unsearchable power of the Creator.
For this reason he brought man in last, after the creation of the creatures.

Not that he was cast aside into corners and outskirts as something contemptible, but rather, as king of those beneath him, he was established as sovereign and master at his very creation. And just as a good host preparing a supper does not bring a guest into his house before the delicacies and foods have been prepared,

but first beautifies, adorns, prepares and makes resplendent with fitting ornament the house and the banquet hall and the couches, and the chairs and seats, variously adorned and beautified, and the tables laden with foods and provisions of many kinds, and when he has thus made the banquet and supper desirable, only then receives the guests,
in the same way that rich one, who delights our nature with most costly provisions and pleasures, beautified this world with every beauty,

and prepared this great and manifold banquet and supper, and only then brought man in, and appointed as his task not the acquiring of what he did not possess, but the enjoyment [?] of what had been bestowed.

And for this reason, because of his twofold constitution, he also sowed twofold causes in him, and mingled the earthly with the divine, so that in both respects, properly and distinctly, he might have a twofold and corresponding enjoyment:

that is, the appropriation of the divine nature through the incorporeal nature, which is the soul; and the enjoyment of the good things of the earth through the bodily and earthly senses, which are the body.
Chapter 3. That the creation and nature of man is more honorable than all visible creation. But we ought not to pass over this either without examining it,

for this world, such as it is, and the material things of its parts, brought forth to complete its whole constitution, were created by the divine power swiftly and without deliberation, all at once, by command alone.
But for the creation of man a deliberation is shown, and what is to be is sketched out beforehand by the Craftsman through a depiction in words:
both what sort of being he ought to be, and to what archetypal form he bears likeness, and for what purpose he should be made, and

What he is to become, what he is to do, and over whom he is to rule: all this the Word deliberates beforehand. And so, before his creation, honor was given to him, and before he came into being he was appointed ruler over the things that exist, for it says:
"And God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness,
and let them rule over the fish of the sea, and the beasts of the earth, and the birds of the sky, and the cattle, and all the earth."
O wonder! The sun was created, and no deliberation about it was set forth; and likewise the heaven, to which what is equal among created things!

And such a marvel came forth by word alone, and the Word indicated neither whence nor how, nor anything else of the kind about it; and likewise all the material things of heaven, each one in turn, that is:
the ether, the stars, and this air spread out between them, and the sea and the dry land, and the animals and the plants and the saplings: all these were created by a word.

But the creation of man alone did the Creator of all set forth with deliberation. He prepared beforehand the material of his constitution, and assigned to him a likeness to that archetypal form and beauty, and he set before himself the purpose, the favor for the sake of which he intended his creation,
so that he might create his nature conformed, suited and fitted to his works, and so that man might be proper to and in keeping with the ordinances laid out before him.
Chapter 4, that the creation of man signifies in every respect the authority of rule. For just as in this life an instrument is fashioned by craftsmen in conformity with its use, in the same way,

like a kind of vessel fitted for royal works, the Architect of all created our nature, with excellence of soul and with the constitution of the body, so that its constitution should be such as is fitting and becoming to kingship. For its freedom and self-mastery make plain and display the sovereignty and loftiness of the soul, since it is a stranger to servile form and to baseness, and is governed by its own will and authority. And who else has such a rank except a king?

And besides this, to be created in the image of that almighty nature is nothing other than for the nature to be prepared at once as a king. For just as, according to human custom, those who prepare an image of rulers portray the likeness of the form,
and adorn that royal image with a garment of purple,
which makes manifest the honor of kings,

and thus the image too is called king, so also human nature, since it was being prepared as ruler over the others, adorned with the likeness of the King of all, as a kind of living image, was thus raised up to share with the archetype both in name and in honor. It was not clothed in purple, nor did it proclaim the honor of kingship by a royal scepter and crown, for neither does the archetype consist in these. Instead of purple it was clothed with virtue, which is more honorable than all royal adornments, and instead of a scepter it was strengthened by the blessedness of immortality,
and so, adorned in every respect with royal honor, it was exactly like that archetypal beauty.
Chapter 5,

That man is like that divine kingship. But the divine beauty does not shine forth through the acquisition of any form or color or coloring; rather, it is seen in that inexpressible blessedness of the virtues.
And just as painters depict human forms on panels by means of colors and pigments, and by their proper and matching pigments soften and blend the likeness,
so that the archetypal image may be depicted exactly through that likeness and representation, so understand it also concerning our Creator: for, as if by colors,
by the brilliance of the virtues he made his image bloom in likeness to his own beauty, in order to display his own sovereignty in us.
But many in form and diverse are those colors of the image by which the true archetypal image is depicted: not purple and bright,
nor their fair bloom blended together, nor eyebrows and eyes drawn with some [?] of blackness and with some coloring of depth and height, nor pigments that shade the face and the garment,

nor as many other such things as the hands [?] of painters skillfully contrive. Instead of these it had purity and freedom from passion and blessedness and estrangement from all evil, and as many things as are like these,
through which the divine likeness is depicted among human beings. And with such flowers of his own image the Creator depicted and adorned this nature of ours.
And if you also examine that other aspect, by which the divine beauty is depicted, you will find that with respect to it, too, the likeness is true,
depicted in our image. Mind and word, then, is the Godhead, for it says: "In the beginning was the Word."

And since those like Paul have the mind of Christ, who speaks in them, humanity too is not far from these things, for you see within yourself both word and mind, in the likeness of that true Mind and Word.

Again, God is love and also the source of love, as the great John says: "Love is from God, and God is love." And the Fashioner of natures has given the capacity for this to us as well, as he says: "By this all will know
that you are my disciples, if you love one another." And whoever lacks this has corrupted the whole likeness of the image.

The Godhead sees all things and hears all things and searches out all things. You too have the perception of created things through what is seen and what is heard, and a mind that judges and searches out the things that exist.
Chapter 6: An investigation of the mind in relation to the property of nature,
in which the heresy of the Anomoeans is briefly refuted. And let no one suppose that I speak of the Godhead after the manner of human activities,
as though the Godhead were divided among manifold powers and activities and conditions; for in the simple nature of the Godhead it is impossible to see those manifold activities and various [?],
for not even in us are minds and understandings divided among manifold activities and powers. For although we come into contact with this life in many ways through the senses,

But one power is established in us, that is, the mind which is in us, which passes out to each of the senses, lays hold of the structure of existing things, and makes it its own. This mind sees created things through the organs of sight.
It perceives speech through the organs of hearing, loves what is lovable, turns away from what is hateful and undesirable, and with the hand does whatever it wishes,
and by it takes hold of things and puts them away, and whatever it judges to be better, that too it does with the assistance of the organ.

Now then, if in man, although the organs prepared by nature for the senses are of many kinds, it is the mind alone that acts and moves through them all, and in the manner suited to each one it manages and makes use of what lies before it,
and it is one and remains the same, and does not change its nature through those varied activities,
how could anyone imagine in God a manifold division of nature on account of those manifold powers,

since he who made the eyes and planted the ears, as a figure and form of himself, portrayed these powers, like certain signs and tokens, in the nature of human beings: "Let us make man in our image and likeness"!

Where now, then, is the heresy of the Anomoeans? What will they say to such a utterance as this, or how will they establish the novelty of their blasphemy in the face of these words? Or are they able to say that many differing persons are made like one image?
And if the Son is unlike the Father by nature, how does he fashion one image of those differing natures?

For he who said "in our image," and by the declaration of many persons indicated the Holy Trinity, would not have displayed the singleness of the image if those archetypal forms were unlike one another,
for it was not possible for things unlike one another to display a single likeness; but if the natures had been of many kinds,
their images too would undoubtedly have been created of many kinds, portrayed in correspondence with one another. But since the image is one, and the archetype is not one,
who would be so far out of his mind as not to know that things which are like one thing are undoubtedly also like one another?
And perhaps it was for this reason that the word said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness": that it might scrape this obstinacy of wickedness out of human life.

Chapter 7. Why man was created naked of natural coverings and weapons. But what is the form of this human constitution and of its upright stance, or why did the powers of bodily life not grow up along with it,

but it is naked of natural coverings, unarmed and poor, and without resource for all its needs? Indeed, it is brought into the world so wretched, and on account of its visible form it is worthy of pity rather than of being called blessed; for it has neither the weapon of horns, nor sharpness of nails, nor of talons, nor of shanks [?],
nor of teeth, nor any deadly dart filled with natural venom,
as many animals have on their heads, to take vengeance on those who trouble them; nor is his flesh covered with a covering of hair. And perhaps someone may even say:
"He who was appointed ruler over the others ought to have been equipped by nature with his own natural weapons, so that he would not need help from anyone else to defend himself.
But as it is, the lion and the boar and the tiger and the leopard, and whatever else is of this kind, have by nature sufficient strength for their own survival,
and the bull has horns, and the hare swiftness, and the gazelle leaping and looking around and a keen, watchful sharpness of eyes, and some other animal has size,
and another a trunk, and birds have wings, and the bee a sting, and to all of them, in every respect, some one natural weapon has been given by God for their survival,
but man alone, of all of them, stands by himself:

slower than the swift runners, smaller than the bulky, more naked than those armed by nature." And perhaps someone will say: "And how has such a creature been appointed to rule over all!" But, as I think, it is not difficult to show that this supposed deficiency of our nature proves to be the reason for our greater rule over those beneath him. For,
if man had such strength that he outstripped the horse in speed,

and had firm, unwearing feet, raised up on soles and shanks, and had horns and stings and claws and sharp nails, then, first, he would be something beastlike and hard to approach because of such a constitution,
and second, he would have disdained rule over the others, since he would need no help from those beneath him and would not be in want of their service.

But as it is, for this reason, the resources of this life, which fill up our deficiencies, were distributed individually among those yoked to us, and this made rule over them unavoidable and necessary.
For the heaviness and slowness of our bodies introduced the use of the horse, and tended and tamed it,
and the nakedness of our bodies made the raising of sheep a necessary concern, for they fill up the deficiency of our nature by giving wool year after year.
And because the means of our life had to be procured from elsewhere as well, burden-bearing animals were appointed to perform such service,
and since we could not graze on the meadow as cattle do, oxen were made subject to our life, so that by their labors they might provide for its deficiency.

And since we also needed the work of teeth and biting, so that they might help us against the other animals by seizing them with the teeth, we were given the dog, along with its swiftness, so that by its constitution it might fulfill our need and be for people like a kind of living sword.
And iron, stronger and more cutting than the sharpness of horns and claws, was devised for people,
which does not stay with us permanently, as these do with beasts, but helps us at the proper time and then remains again in its own place.
And in place of the crocodile's hide, that very thing itself becomes armor for those who put on its hide in time of battle.
But if not, in like manner iron is prepared by craftsmen, which serves us in time of battle,

and again, it frees the armed man from its weight, so that in time of peace he may live freely and at rest. And again, the feathers of birds likewise also serve our life, so that through contrivance we may not fall short even of their height,
for some of them become tame and helpers to hunters, and others by their own bodies supply what we need.
And again, by the device of flying arrows, skill equips us, and by means of the bow it grants us the height of the birds for our use.
And so that we may walk in comfort and without injury, it makes the help of the creatures beneath us necessary, for from them leather [?] and footwear are prepared for our feet.

Chapter 8. Why the form of man was created upright, and that the hands exist for the sake of speech, in which he also sets forth philosophy concerning the distinction of souls. But the form of man was created upright, looking toward heaven and raised upward,
and this too is the bearing of rule and depicts the honor of kingship,
for among beings man alone is clothed with such a form,
whereas in all the others the bending of the body toward the earth makes clear the difference in honor: between those who serve a power and the one who stands over them with authority.

For in all the others the front arms are given as feet, so that they may be a firm support and bearer for their stooping posture, but in the constitution of man those feet of the animals were made into hands,
for to the upright form one footing, securely established by the two feet, was sufficient for use.
And again, the service of the hands assists the power of speech and its usefulness,
and if anyone should call the service of the hands proper and peculiar to rational nature, he would not be wrong. And do not bring your mind only to what is common and known to all, that is,
that by the training and intelligence of the hands, and by the forming of letters, we write down speech.

For neither is this without a share in the graces of eloquence, nor foreign to them: our speaking and conversing through writings, when we join speech to letters and, as it were, converse by means of the hand.

But I am speaking of the help of the hands toward another form as well, which is the vocal articulation of speech. However, before investigating this matter, let us investigate the remaining subject, for according to the order of creation it had almost passed us by:
the statement of it, namely, for what reason the sprouting of the earth's plants came first, and then that of beasts and cattle, and then, last of all and after them, the creation of man,
for we do not understand from this only that God created plants for the sake of animals, and animals for the sake of men,
and that before the cattle their foods were created, and before man those things that were to serve human life.
Rather, I think that by these matters Moses reveals a certain hidden teaching and an ineffable philosophy of the soul, which outside learning also dreamed of, but did not clearly understand.
And by this he teaches us that the form of life is seen in three divisions: the ensouled, the moving, and the spiritual.

And the first is only growing and nourished, and it supplies in a fitting way the power of nourishment to what is nourished and grows. It is also called natural, and it is seen among plants and among vegetation as a certain power of life,
having no share in sense-perception. But apart from this there is another form of life, which has this as well and has in addition received governance through the senses,
and which is observed in the nature of irrational animals, for they are not only nourished and grow, but also have the power and aid of sense-perception.

But the perfect life in bodies is seen among rational beings, that is, in human nature alone, for it is nourished and perceives and speaks and is governed by the mind. Hence let us introduce some such statement as a division of beings,
for some are incorporeal and some corporeal. But as for the division of the incorporeal and intellectual, let the discussion await its proper time, for our discussion is not about that.
Of these corporeal things, some have no share of life at all, while some receive the power of life.
And again, of those living bodies, some live by sense-perception and some are strangers to sense-perception, and that which perceives is in turn divided into rational and irrational.

For this reason, first, after those soulless material things, which are heaven and earth and the luminaries and the waters, the lawgiver presented this natural life, as a kind of step and foundation for the constitution of animate beings,
which was created first in plants and vegetation, and then he added the creation of those that live by sense-perception.
And since, after them, for those constituted with bodily life, even without the incorporeal nature,

it is possible to live on one's own by sense-perception alone, whereas the life of a rational being is impossible without the body, and unless the corporeal is blended with that incorporeal nature, therefore last of all,
after plants and irrational animals, man was created, and through progress step by step he rose to the perfection of nature,

and man, this rational living being, shares in all the forms of ensoulment and motion, for he is nourished in the manner of the animate life of plants, and to the power of growth he has joined the perceptive power,
and by its own nature it holds a middle way between the invisible and the material essence, and it is as much coarser than the one as it is purer than the other.

And then there came about, with that fine and light-colored and invisible nature, which is the intellectual essence, a certain appropriation and blending and kinship, so that in this way man might have his constitution and being from these three,
as we have learned from the Apostle, for in the Epistle to the Ephesians he prays for them for the full vitality and grace of the body,
of the soul and of the spirit, to be preserved at the coming of the Lord; for he called the growing part body, the perceiving part soul, and the intellectual part spirit.
And likewise the Lord in the Gospel taught that scribe to reckon the love of God as higher than every commandment, which is fulfilled with all the heart and mind and spirit,

For here too the same division is indicated: he called the structure of the body "heart," presented the soul as the animating principle and the middle term, and proclaimed the mind to be the higher nature, the rational and understanding power.

And likewise the Apostle knows a division of three wills. One he names carnal, which is the parent of gluttony, ease and love of pleasure; the second, soulish, which is midway between virtue and wickedness, higher than the one,
but not attaining fully and purely to the other; and the third, spiritual, in which the perfection of the divine way of life is seen.
Therefore he speaks to the Corinthians and reproaches their luxury and passion, saying in effect: "You are carnal" and unable to take in perfect teachings.
And again, in another place he makes a comparison of the middle with the perfect and says: "The soulish man does not receive the things of the Spirit,
for they are foolishness to him; but the spiritual man judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one."
For just as the soulish is superior to the carnal, so in the same way the spiritual is higher than the soulish.

And if the book speaks of the creation of man as a living soul last of all, after everything else, this means nothing other than that the lawgiver is philosophizing and teaching us about the soul: that, through a certain unavoidable sequence of orders, he sees its perfection in what comes last. For together with rationality it has gathered into itself the remaining orders as well, and together with sensation it undoubtedly has a share in what belongs to plants too.
But the latter is seen only through material things.
Therefore, as if by ladders and steps, which are the properties of life, nature makes its ascent from the lower to the more perfect.

Chapter 9. That the form of man was prepared like an instrument for the use of speech. And since man is a rational living being, the instrument of the body had to be prepared in conformity with speech. For,
just as musicians play their music according to the kind of instrument, and neither pipe on lyres nor play the harp on pipes,
so in the same way the structure of the instrument had to be arranged in conformity with speech, so that, shaped by the vocal members, it might sound aptly for the use and employment of words.

And for this reason hands were joined to the body. For although countless uses in life can be enumerated for which this resourceful and highly skilled instrument of the hands has aptitude and special fitness,
and however many deeds and mighty works of war and peace they readily accomplish, yet above every other task nature added them to the body for the sake of the gift of speech.
For if man had been without a share of hands, then undoubtedly the structure of his face would have been prepared like that of the quadrupeds, in conformity with their way of taking food,
so that the face would be elongated and narrowed at the nostrils,
and the lips attached to the mouth would be [?]-like, thick and hard, suited for grazing on pasture; and he would have had a tongue of the same kind, rough and hard and a helper to the teeth,

or else moist and thin and lying round about, as is that of dogs and of the other flesh-eaters, so that along with the [?] of the teeth and the gaps between them it might pass to and fro in the consuming of food.

For if there were no hands on the body, how could it have been given an articulate voice, when the structure of the parts of the mouth would not have been made suited to the use of speech and voice, but rather bellowing, or bleating, or barking would have been unavoidable and necessary,
or the neighing of a horse, or lowing like oxen and cows, or the letting out of some beastlike roar.
But now, since hands have been set on the body and joined to the structure of the flesh, the structure of the mouth has been fitted and adorned for the service of speech.
Therefore the hands have been made ready as something proper and peculiar to the rational nature, for thus the Creator arranged it for the ease of speech.

And since the Creator graciously bestowed divinely beautiful graces on our being and imprinted the likeness of his own good things in his image, for this reason he granted those other good things to human nature as a gift,
but wisdom and understanding he did not grant as a gift; rather, he gave them.

That is to say, he clothed his own image with the adornment of his own nature. And since the mind is bodiless and fleshless, its grace would have been incommunicable and unmingled if some stirring and means did not make its movement apparent.

For this reason this organ-like formation of man became necessary, so that the mind might touch the voice-producing members as a plectrum does, and through the quality of the voice and its shaping might interpret the inner stirring,
and just as a skilled musician who, because of some ailment, does not have a voice of his own,

but wishes to make his art known, so too the human mind is a discoverer of various thoughts, which it cannot bring forth through the bodily senses, nor reveal the stirrings of the mind by the naked soul; therefore,
like a skilled musician it touches these living instruments, and by the sound coming from them it makes known its hidden intentions.
For the human instrument is blended, by sharing in the sounds of music, with the pipe and the flute, as if by some mutual concord of things speaking together,
for the breath, forced out of the parts and the breathing vessels, when the will of the speaker has set firmly to making sound, is stirred into sound by inner strikings,

and then, when it fills the surrounding pipe-like channels of the nostrils, it resembles the sound given out by a flute, and from those thin and fine outlets all around it lets out a whistling, and the palate receives in its own hollow that sound rising from the depth and directs it toward the [?] passages leading out from the nose,
and as if through flutes it softens and strengthens the sound,
while the cheeks and the tongue and the structure of the throat and that channel of the [?] are hollowed and sharpen the sound,

And all this that [?] string-striker displays through the sinews in diverse and many-colored ways, and in an instant and swiftly it tunes those strings of music as it wishes; and the opening and closing of the lips displays the same pattern as the placing and lifting of the fingers on pipes, by which they make a way for the breath to go out according to the harmony of the music.
Thus, then, through this organ-like structure the mind plays speech within us, on account of which we were created rational; and, as I think,
we would not have received this grace of speech if we had to procure for the body, with our lips, the heavy and burdensome necessity of the service of food.
But as it is, the hands have taken such service upon themselves, and have made the mouth unhindered for the service of speech and left it free.

Chapter 10: That the mind works through the bodily senses. And through this human organ a twofold activity is seen: the one for producing the voice, and the other for receiving outward perceptions; and the one is not confused with the other,
but each stands at the task appointed to it by nature and does not disturb its neighbor:

neither hearing disturbs speech, nor speech hearing. For the one is always speaking and does not cease, while the ear continually receives and is not filled, as Solomon says. For this reason we ought to marvel all the more
at what that inner receiving space is, into which everything poured in through the hearing enters.
Who are the recorders, for remembrance, of the words entering into it, or what kind of treasuries are they that receive the understandings which have come in through the ears,
or how is it that, when so many diverse and mutually similar words enter into it, no confusion and error arises from their being received one upon another and from each being set in its place?
And equally with this we ought to marvel at the eyes too, for likewise, in a similar way, through them as well the mind goes outside the body,

and lays hold of the likeness of things that appear and draws it to itself, and inscribes the images of visible things within itself. And just as a city ruling many lands receives through its various entrances the peoples who come to it,
and they do not all gather together in one place of the city, but some go to the marketplace, some to houses, others to church, and others to a neighborhood,
or hurry to streets and alleys and theaters and spectacles, and each one yields to his own will,
so too I see the city of the mind built within us,
which the various entrances of the senses fill, while the mind examines and distinguishes each of those entering, and assigns them to the places of its knowledge according to what suits them.
And as is seen in the example of the city, for often certain tribes and kindreds,
who do not enter by one gate, but one enters there from one side and another by another, as it happens, are found to be in no way less inside the wall, and are again together with one another,
and associate with one another; and again the reverse of this also happens,
For strangers and people unknown to one another often enter the city by one gate, yet entering together and sharing that entry does not unite them with one another,
for even after they have gone inside, they are able to part from one another and go off to their own people. I see something of this same kind in the expanse of the mind,
for often it gathers for us one knowledge from senses of various kinds, when one and the same thing is divided into many parts with respect to the senses. And likewise the reverse is also seen,
for from one single sense it teaches us things of many kinds, which are not one by nature.

And it is better that I make this statement clear by an illustration. Let the matter before us, then, be the inquiry into the distinction of tastes: which is sweet to the senses, or which is to be shunned by those who discern taste.
The bitterness of gall and the savor of honey are known from experience, and these are evident and bring in a single knowledge,
but that one thing is assigned to the mind in many parts, that is, to tasting, smelling, hearing, touching and seeing.
For when someone sees honey, and hears its name, and tastes its flavor, and smells its fragrance, and examines it with the hand, he perceives that one thing through each of the senses. And again,
through one sense we learn many things of many forms, for the ears receive all sounds, and the power of sight remains undivided in seeing distinct objects,
for the eyes perceive white and black together, and all things that are distinguished by color,
and so too with taste, and so too with smell, and so too with the power of touch: each obtains and displays the perception of things of diverse kinds according to its own capacity.
Chapter 11,

that the nature of the mind is invisible. What then is the mind according to its own nature, which divides itself out to the powers of the senses and through each of them fittingly receives the understanding of existing things?
And that the mind is something other than and apart from the senses, no reasonable person disputes, because if it were one of the senses,
it would surely have only one activity and property of perception, because it is simple, and in what is simple no multiplicity is seen.
But as it is, it is mingled with all of them, though they are separated from one another, for touch is one thing and smell another, and the rest likewise have no share in one another and are unmixed.

And since it is seen alongside each one in a manner fitting to each and on equal terms with each, its nature must surely be understood as something other, apart from the senses, so that no multiplicity or density may be mingled with that intellectual and simple nature.
The Apostle says: "Who has known the mind of the Lord?" But I say: who has known his own mind, or who has examined it?
Tell, then, those who subject the divine nature to their own understanding and comprehension: have they examined themselves?
Or do they know the nature of their own mind? Is it perhaps of many parts, of many structures and of many members?

And how can the intelligent thing be compounded, or what is this strange form of the mixing and joining of forms? Then is it perhaps simple and uncompounded? But how is it dispersed among these many-parted senses,
how is multiformity seen in what is simple, or how is singleness seen in what is multiform?

But I found a resource in the midst of helplessness and a solution in the insoluble when I raised myself to the divine voice itself, that is, the one which says: "Let us make man in our image and likeness."

For as long as an image lacks nothing of its archetypal image, so long is it truly called an image; but in whatever way it falls away from likeness to the archetype, in that respect it is no longer an image.

Now therefore, since one of the properties of the divine nature is the incomprehensibility of its nature and essence, it is altogether undeniable that the image too, in this respect, should have likeness to the archetypal image.
For if the nature of the image were comprehended while the archetypal image were beyond comprehension, that contrast in this respect would make manifest and expose the deficiency of the image;
but since our nature, which is the image of the Creator, escapes the knowledge and comprehension of the mind, it holds a true likeness to that transcendent nature,
and by its own unknowability it portrays that incomprehensible nature.

Chapter 12: In which members the ruling mind should be supposed to reside, in which he speaks of the natural philosophy of tears and laughter, and that the mind is contained neither in the head nor in the heart, and concerning the natural communion of matter, nature, and mind with one another. Let, then, all the conjectural vain talk of those cease
who confine the intelligent and invisible power of the mind within certain bodily members, some of whom assign it to be in the heart, while others say that
the mind dwells in the head, and they support such conjectures by many devices.
For the one who places the ruling mind in the heart makes the position of the heart the sign of his argument, since it is thought that it occupies the middle place of the whole body,
so that by that self-governing movement it may easily be distributed from the middle to the whole body, and so proceed to actions.
And as a witness to this argument he brings forward a person's sorrowful and wrathful affection and agitation, for it is thought that perhaps such passions move the heart to softening.
But those who assign the mind to the head speak of the head as having been built by nature as a kind of citadel of the whole body,
and of the mind dwelling in it like a king, surrounded by the senses as by certain servants, messengers, and subjects of his.

And as proof of this arrangement these also point to the disruption of thoughts and the derangement of consciousness if some harm befalls the head, or the brain case and the membrane of the brain, and to the fact that a person becomes ignorant of what is proper when the head grows heavy with drunkenness;
And they add also certain other natural causes for such suspicions concerning the ruling mind, and from both sides they adduce causes of this kind. For the one party says
that the motions of the mind have the property of fire, since both fire and the mind are always in motion, and since it is acknowledged that heat springs up in the organ of the heart.

For this reason it says that the ready mobility of heat is blended with the motions of the mind, and it maintains that the heart, in which the heat is contained, is the treasury of the intelligent nature.
But the others say that the head, with the passages and membranes of the brain and the skin of the head, is as it were the root and foundation of all the senses,

and they make their words credible in this way: that the power of the mind is established nowhere else but in the head, where the ear is implanted and receives the resounding of the sounds that enter it;

and sight likewise, by the extension [?] of the eyes, perceives in the pupils the visible forms and images and conveys them to the depth of the body; and the richnesses of scents, through the smelling of the nostrils, are distinguished in the same place.
And the sense of taste is tested by the discernment of the brain, whose adjoining nerves,
descending from the neck and throat and joined with one another through the passages of the palate, establish the order of the senses.
But I say that it is true that the powers of the soul are disturbed by a certain tyranny of the passions, and that the thoughts are weakened in their natural power by some bodily affliction.
And I acknowledge the heart to be the source of the heat of the body and the mover toward the impulses of anger.

And again, along with this I say also that the senses are laid beneath the head and the brain, according to the word of those who speak of such things, who by themselves make the head their own [?], and its being enriched by the vapours that come from them.
And whatever those who speak of such things have said from experience, I do not despise;
yet I do not accept this as a token and sign that the incorporeal nature is confined and circumscribed in a place. For derangement of mind comes about not only from drunkenness,
but also from [?] and from the pain and smarting of the sides.
Likewise those experienced in medicine speak of the derangement of the mind which they call delirium.
And the entry of pain into the heart from grief they have understood mistakenly,
for it is not the heart but the mouth of the stomach that becomes hardened, and out of inexperience they attribute that affliction to the heart.

And those who know the power of these affections by experience say the following: that from excessive griefs the passages and channels of the body, which nature possesses, are closed and separated, and all of them turn toward the depths of the body and are held back from going out.

Hence the breathing of the inward parts is constricted by the vapours shut up within them, and it is by force that nature draws in air to widen and open the closed and constricted inward parts. And such exhalations, brought on by grief, they name sighing and groaning and forced exhalation. And the constriction that is supposed to be on the side of the heart is not of the heart,
But the distaste of the stomach arises from the same cause,
which is the disturbance and blocking of the pores and channels, when that bitter and burning bile pours out from the bile-collecting vessels into the mouth of the stomach.

And this is known from the following: the color of the afflicted person turns yellow, his flesh becomes saffron-like, and his mouth, from that excessive malignancy, spreads the bitter taste of the bile to the veins.

And again, in the same way, the opposite affection, that of joy and laughter, confirms this argument still more, for from joy the pores of the body spread open and are loosened at the hearing of something desirable, and they grow rich and swollen.

For just as in the former case, from grief, the fine and invisible breathing passages of the pores are blocked, constrict the structure of the inner bowels, and send up a moist vapor to the head and the regions of the brain, and this vapor, once it has settled for a short time in the hollows of the head, then changes into water and pours out from those hidden channels toward the eyes, drawn by the contracting of the brows,
and it comes out to the pores of the eyes in the form of drops, and those drops are called tears.

In the same way, understand the opposite kind as well: when the pores are widened more than usual and breath is drawn through them into the depth of the body, and from there nature drives it out again through all the bowels to the pores of the mouth, and especially through the liver, which, as they say, by certain turnings and boiling-like movements forces such breath to go out. Therefore nature contrives some ease for this going out of the breath: it widens the pores of the mouth and on both sides, through the vapor, spreads apart [?] the cheeks. And such a thing is called laughter.
Yet the ruling mind is not for this reason to be ascribed to the liver, nor, on account of the boiling of the blood around the heart that comes about through anger,
-- to the heart; rather, all this pertains to the condition of the structure of the body,

while the mind is blended equally with each member by a certain ineffable blending. Even if some put Scripture before us on this matter, as though it testified that the mind exists in the heart, we shall not accept this without examination, for he who mentioned the hearts did not pass over the kidneys either, but spoke thus:
"God, who judges the hearts and kidneys." Therefore they must confine the rational mind either in both or in neither.
But when I learn of a dulling of the powers of the mind, or even their complete inactivity, through a change in the condition of the body,
I do not consider this a sufficient sign for confining the power of the mind to any particular place,

nor would I attribute its inactivity to its being constricted out of its proper space and made inactive by the inflammation of certain parts of the body; for this is a property of the substance of the body, that through the swelling and corruption of the members they corrupt their own structure,

For the invisible and intelligent nature is neither shut up in the depth of the flesh nor corrupted along with what has grown thick and swollen. Rather, since the whole body is prepared like an instrument of some kind of music, it is as often happens with someone skilled in music or song who is unable to display his own art,
when the damaged state of the instrument does not admit his art,

when it has either decayed through length of time, or is broken or cracked, or has been made useless by some venom or by moths and worms, and for these reasons is useless and unmusical, even though the art of the piper or of the string-player [?] blows or strikes intelligently and knowledgeably. In the same way the mind also reaches to the whole instrument and,
in a manner suited to the powers of the mind, as is fitting, touches each member, and in those that remain in their natural order it performs its own works,
but in those that have been weakened and cannot receive its skilful action, it becomes useless and idle.
For the mind is at home with those that remain in their natural state, but becomes a stranger to those that have been altered from it.
And, as I think, a certain natural concord is seen through this matter, through which some lofty teaching and understanding is made known to us.
For since the most beautiful and highest good of all is God himself, toward whom everything looks,

whatever has a desire for the good, therefore we say also of the mind, which was created as the image of that good, the best of goods, that as long as it partakes of the beauty of the original likeness, as far as is possible,

it too abides in the good; but if it separates from it and falls away from it, it is stripped of the goodness in which it was. And, as we have said, the adornment of the mind by likeness to that original goodness is like a mirror
beautified by the image of what is seen in it; in the same way we say that the nature governed by the mind is a likeness of the mind,

and we understand that it too is beautified by the goodness that comes from the mind. For it becomes like a mirror of a mirror, and it holds and governs the constitution of this material person and substance in which nature is seen.
And as long as they are united with one another, in harmony throughout, they advance by participation in that true good, and these lower things are beautified by the one that is higher.
But if some severance of this good union occurs, or this order is reversed and the superior becomes inferior to the inferior,
then the natural ugliness of matter itself is exposed when it is left alone, for the substance of matter is in itself formless and unprepared.

And thus, through its ugliness, the beauty of nature, which is adorned by the mind, is destroyed along with it; and then the stain of matter and its loathsomeness is passed on through nature to the mind itself, until the image of God is no longer seen in the likeness of the creature.

For when the mind, like a mirror, turns the image of good things to its back, it puts away from itself the pattern and color of the brightness of the good, and gathers into itself the formlessness of matter; and in this way the beginning of evil is born,
and it receives its existence through separation from the good. But as much as anything is made akin to the head of good things, all such is good,

and as much as it is separated from his love and communion and kinship, it is without share in every good. Now therefore, since, according to this argument, the true good is God alone, and the mind was created in his image, and as long as it remains in its likeness to the image,
it too is good through him; and nature, which is encompassed and strengthened by the mind, being a kind of image of the image, has been made known by these things:
that our material being is established and stands firm as long as it is governed by nature,
and likewise, again, it is dissolved and falls when it is separated from what holds it and strengthens it, and is cut off from union with the good.
And this does not happen otherwise than when nature turns toward the side of the opposite and its desire does not advance toward the good,

but when it is in need of one who adorns it, and when it is deprived of the one who makes it beautiful. For when nature has been impoverished of its own beauty, it becomes formless and ugly, away from its likeness to the image.

And this was investigated by us as a consequence of something that entered into the present argument. For what we had to investigate was this: whether the rational power of the mind is established in certain parts of the body, or whether it reaches all of them equally. For

those who confine the mind in particular local parts, and who, to establish such a supposition, adduce the mind's failure to function properly as a result of disturbance and change in certain places of the brain and afflicted places — the argument has shown, however,

that in all the parts of the human body, in which each member is established and governed, the power of the soul is equally inactive in all of them if those parts do not remain in accordance with nature.
And thus, as a consequence of these things, the argument stated above entered in, by which we understand this concerning the human being and body: that the mind is governed by God,
and this material life of ours by the mind, when it remains in accordance with nature; but if it is shaken and turned away from nature, it also becomes estranged from the power and help of the mind.

But let us return to the point from which we departed. For if the parts of the body have not been changed from their natural order by some affliction, the mind displays its own power and acts, and it is alive and vigorous in those that are firm,

and likewise, again, it is powerless in those that cannot contain its actions and powers. It would have been possible to prove this teaching and make it credible from another side as well, if we had not been hindered by the heaviness of ears and the weariness of listening to words; but let us add what is lacking, as far as we are able, in brief.

Chapter 13. An explanation of the causes of sleep and yawning and dreams. This material and river-like life of the flesh always proceeds by motion, and in this it has the power of its being, that it never stops moving. For like a river, which travels within its own bounds and fills the track of its own channel wherever it goes,
and the water of that river does not stay altogether in one place, but some of it has gone and flowed away, while some of it is arriving and coming on,
so too the materiality of this life, through a certain motion and flow arising from the conjunction and succession of opposing things, does not rest, and it can never cease from change.
But if it should ever rest from motion, it will undoubtedly rest from being and from life as well. Understand it in this way: emptying receives filling, and fullness comes in after emptying.
Satiety fills up hunger, and hunger follows upon satiety. Sleep softens the strain of wakefulness, and again, wakefulness braces the slackness of sleep, and none of these remains forever,
but at the coming of the one the other withdraws, and they give way to each other, and in this way nature renews itself by their exchange,
so that through the succession of each in turn, the exchange between them and the passing from one side to the other may be uninterrupted. For constant tension of a living creature in its activities
brings tearing and severing upon the limbs and parts forcibly stretched, and again, complete rest of the flesh slackens and brings down the firmness of body and mind.
But an orderly succession of both from time to time gives power to nature and strengthens it, as it constantly passes over to opposites, each side giving itself rest by means of the other.

Thus, then, it takes the body strained by wakefulness and gives it rest through sleep, and grants timely leisure to the labor of the senses, like horses unharnessed after the race and contest of the chariots.

For timely rest is necessary and indispensable for the firmness of the structure of the flesh, so that it may spread the power of nourishment without hindrance through the whole body by means of its passages, and so that no opposition from the strain of wakefulness may strike against that dissemination. For just as from moist earth,
when the heat of the sun warms it, certain mist-like vapors rise from the depths like smoke,
so something similar happens in this earth of ours as well, when food boils up within from the natural heat.
And since vapors imitate air and by nature go upward, they are carried by their upward rise to the regions of the head, like some smoke

that has entered a crack in a wall, and then from there they divide toward the passages of the senses and spread out and grow light. Hence, as the vapors pass out, the senses are of necessity made idle,
for the eyes stick to the eyelids, as though weighed down by some device of lead, and they let the lids fall over the eyes.

And likewise, by those same vapors the hearing is thickened, and as if with a kind of door they shut the organs of hearing and fall upon the ears, and these rest from their natural power and activity. And this kind of condition is called sleep,

because of the rest and immobility of the bodily senses and their complete idleness from natural movement, so that the passage to and fro and the dissolving of the food may be easy, when those vapors go out through each of the pores and are dissipated.

And for this reason the structure of the senses is constricted by those inner vapors, and if sleep is held off by some compulsion, the vein-like pores are filled and by nature become strained beyond measure and are stretched out,
and so that the part thickened by that stretching may be relieved of those vapors, nature has for this reason devised the practice of yawning, so that, just as those do
who forcibly press water out of garments by twisting and [?],

and since that part of the throat is rounded and its air vessels are many, when that thickened vapor goes out from there, since a straight exit from the winding and rounded parts is impossible unless it is stretched out by a turning movement,

for this reason the breath of yawning, having remained in the depths of the body, is emptied out of the parts of the body by that going out of breath, from that thickening of the rich matter, and departs.
And this often happens after sleep, when some of those thick vapors remain in certain places undissolved and not breathed out.
And in this way the human mind clearly becomes known, for it acts in concert with nature: as long as nature stands alert and wakeful, the mind too acts and moves,
but when nature is released by sleep, the mind remains motionless, unless some marvel coming from dreams, which occurs in sleep, should attribute movement to the mind.
But we say that only the acts of the prudent and understanding mind ought to be attributed to the mind,
while the imaginary ravings in sleep we name a likeness and shadow of the acts of the mind, and we attribute their formation and invention to the animal part of the soul,
for when the soul is released from the senses by sleep, it involuntarily withdraws also from the activities of the mind and departs,
for it is through these that the mind is mingled with man,

and when the senses fall silent, the mind too is of necessity idle. And the sign of this is the following: the one undergoing this in sleep imagines that he has fallen into a marvel of unseemly and impossible things, which would not happen if reason and mind were governing the soul at that time. But, as I think,
at that time those more principal powers of the soul rest from the power of the mind and from sensation and movement, while that part [?] of growth labors and acts in sleep,
and certain forms and images and echoes produced in it during wakefulness through the senses also lay claim to the action of the mind,
and these are imprinted in it by the part of the soul that holds memory. And such imperfect images and vain echoes remain in that memory-holding form of the soul.
And through such things a person dreams, not devising the images shown to him in any coherent order, but led astray and cut up this way and that by a certain mingled, muddled and incoherent delusion.

For just as in the working of the body, when each of the parts labors separately, according to the natural power that is within them, a certain sharing arises between the member that is quieted [?] and at rest and those that are moving and active,
in the same way the soul too is seen: even though some part of it is silent and some part is moving, the whole is joined together with that part,
for it is not possible for its natural unity to be cut apart when the activity of its power is held by some one part. But just as, when people are awake and alert,
the mind is self-governing and rules, while the senses serve, and the power that manages the body is not separated from them, for the mind procures what is needed for nourishment,

the sense receives what has been procured, and the body's power of growth assimilates to itself what is given, so also in sleep the rule of these powers within us is in a certain way changed. And when the irrational part grows strong, the power of the others subsides.

Yet it is not wholly extinguished. And when the power of growth then hastens toward digestion through sleep and keeps the whole of nature occupied with itself, the power of perception is not wholly cut off from it either, for what has once been united cannot be cut apart,
nor is it able to make its power shine forth, for it is bound by the inactivity of the senses caused by sleep.

In the same way, likewise, the mind too, being united with and assigned to the perceiving part of the soul, is rightly said to move when this part moves, and when this part is at rest, to rest and subside along with it,
as happens with fire, when it is covered on every side with chaff and has no outlet for the flame to blaze up:
it neither burns the chaff nor is wholly extinguished, but instead of flame it sends up a kind of vapor and smoke into the air; but if it finds some outlet,

it turns the smoke into flame. In the same way the mind too is covered over in sleep through the inactivity of the senses, and it can neither shine, because of the covering they cause, nor is it wholly extinguished,
but it moves in a smoke-like way, and it does some things and is unable to do others.
And as when a master musician strikes the slackened strings of a lyre with a plectrum, no harmonious sound comes out, for it does not sound sweetly without being stretched and tuned,
even though the craftsman's hand moves skillfully and turns the plectrum in the proper place on the strings, yet there is no sound or tone, but only a certain tasteless and discordant droning,
so too, when through sleep the organ-like apparatus of the senses is slackened, either the artist rests and subsides completely,

if complete slackening and breakdown befalls that organ through some stupor and morbid heaviness, or else he displays his power weakly and faintly, since the organ of the senses does not truly receive his art.

And for this reason, if there is any memory, it is mixed and confused in sleep; and if it lays claim to any foreknowledge, that foreknowledge is doubtful and hidden, imagined in some form and shadow out of the concerns of waking life. And sometimes it announces something that is going to happen, for that subtlety of nature has something beyond the coarseness of the body,
by which it is able to see something of what is to come, yet not simply and openly, by way of speech,

so that its teaching, once presented, and its foretold announcement might be bright and clear, but rather in a certain allusive, implied and doubtful manner, which those who interpret such matters call a riddle. Thus the cupbearer was pressing the cluster of grapes into Pharaoh's cup; thus the baker imagined himself carrying the basket, these being the things each of them applied himself to when awake. Each of them thought that he was engaged in these same things in the dream as well, for the likeness of the activities of their habit,
imprinted on the foreknowing faculty of the soul, after a time gave them a divination of what was to come, through a prophecy of the mind.
But if Daniel and Joseph and those like them were instructed beforehand by divine power in the foreknowledge of things to come,

because no passion confused their senses, this has nothing to do with the present inquiry, for who would there be who would attribute such things to the power of dreams? And if anyone should become so foolish, he would without doubt also regard the revelations of God that occurred to people awake as not being a vision,
but a natural event, happening of itself and by chance.
For just as all people live according to their own mind, and there are only a few who become worthy of divine converse and of clear revelation,

so too all share equally and in common in the naturally produced imagining of dreams. Yet not all dreams are to be ascribed to the revelation of God and to the seeing of visions; rather, even if some foreknowledge from dreams comes to certain people, it happens in the manner described above, that is, as it happened to those servants of Pharaoh.
But if the Egyptian and Assyrian tyrants received from God a revelation of things to come, the dispensation worked through them is another matter,
for it was necessary that the hidden wisdom of the saints be revealed, so that such a benefit should not pass by the common life of humankind without profit.
For how would it have become known that Daniel was such a man, if those sorcerers and magi had not been at a loss in searching out the hidden matter!

Or how would Egypt have been saved, if Joseph had remained in prison and the interpretation of the dream had not brought him forth into the midst! Hence such cases as these must be ascribed to some other dispensation, and not to the common imagining of dreams.
But this customary seeing of dreams is common to all and occurs through imaginings of many forms and many kinds,

for either some imagining and image of daily activities remains in the remembering part of the soul, or, according to the condition of the body, imagination, will and desire are often expressed through dreams as well.

For thus a thirsty person dreams of being at springs, and one in need of food dreams of being at banquets, and for a youth in the vigor of his age, fantasies appear in keeping with his age and the stirring of his passions.
And I know yet another cause of the fantasies of sleep, for I was treating one of our own relatives, who had been struck by derangement,
who was once weighed down beyond measure by eating, and he cried out and accused those standing there, as though they had given him bowels full of dung,
and then, when his body broke into a sweat, he told those present to have water ready, to be sprinkled on the one lying there,
and he did not cease from crying out until the outcome of the matter made known the cause of such accusations;
for immediately copious sweat poured over his body, and his belly was loosened and made evident the heaviness of the bowels,

and so the keenness that had been dulled by the disease, and that burned along with his nature in sympathy with the body's affliction, was not unaware of what was suffered, but because of the derangement it was unable to declare what was distressing it.
And if the disease had not been the cause, but the mind of the soul had been illuminated out of natural sleep, such an utterance of the sick man would have been reckoned a dream or a vision,
for the water would have been interpreted as that river of sweat, and the heaviness of the bowels as that load of food.

And most physicians confirm this same thing, for they say that the dreams of the sick and the seeing of the fantasies of sleep follow the differences of their afflictions: those whose stomach is inflamed see some dreams, and those whose head is inflamed see others,
and those afflicted by fever see others, and those made ill by bile and phlegm see others,
and those tried by fullness of body and by wasting see others. And from all this it is seen
that the nurturing and growing part of the soul's powers [?] has something sown in it by the mind, because of their mingling,
and these conform to the condition of the body, and in accordance with the afflictions
by which they are gripped, they change their fantasies as well.

And likewise again, the dreams of most people also conform to the constitution, habit and kind of their wills; for some dreams belong to the brave, and others to the fearful and cowardly, and some dreams belong to the impure, and others to the pure, and others to the generous and merciful, and other fantasies appear to the greedy and insatiable.

These do not arise from the mind, but it is from the irrational will that such fantasies are imprinted in the soul: the things to which it had grown accustomed through practice in waking life, their very images and forms it depicts in sleep as well.

Chapter 14: That the mind is not in the parts of the body, and on the distinction between bodily and spiritual movements. But we have strayed far from the matter at hand, for the discourse promised to show us
that the mind is not bound to any portions or part of the body,
but is joined to all of them equally, in conformity with nature, and produces the movement and action of the part in which it is.
And it sometimes happens that the mind even submits to natural impulses and becomes like a servant,

For the nature of the flesh often becomes its guide, and it appropriates the perception of what is distressing and the desire for what gladdens. And from such beginnings there first arises [?] in it either the desire for food,

or the inclination toward the arousal of any other desires and toward the love of pleasure; and the mind takes such inclinations and arousals into account, and by its own resourcefulness procures for the flesh the occasions it wishes for and desires.

But this does not happen in everyone, but only in those who have been overcome and taken captive by the passions, who, with the assistance of the mind, have enslaved reason to the impulses of nature, and who fawn like slaves upon the sweetness of the senses.
But with the perfect it does not happen in this way, for the mind leads reason, and it is not the passions that choose what is better, and nature follows in the footsteps of its guide.

Now reason has found three divisions among the forms and powers of life: the first, which grows without sensation; the second, which grows and has sensation but is a stranger to the activities of speech;
and the third, which is rational and perfect and extends to all the powers, which is also present in the others and possesses intelligence beyond them all.

Let no one therefore suppose on this account that three souls are joined together in the human constitution, seen within separate boundaries, and that the creation and perfection of human nature should be thought of as a combining of many souls;
