rather, the true and perfect soul is one, by nature intelligent and immaterial, and through the senses it is united with material nature.

Everything material is subject to change and alteration, and as long as it shares in the animating power, it grows and flourishes; but when it is separated from the power of life, it ends its movement in decay.
And neither can the senses accomplish their activities without material substance, nor can the power of the intelligent mind do so without the senses.
Chapter 15: That the rational soul is truly called soul, and is both called so and is so, while the other souls are called soul only as namesakes and in name;
in which he says that the power of the mind is spread through the whole body and is adapted in conformity with each part. But if one of the created beings has the power of growth,
or if again another is governed by the power of the senses, the former does not have sensation,

nor does the latter have a share in intelligent nature; and therefore let no one suspect a plurality of souls, for this argument cannot show any division of souls. For everything visible among existing things,

if it is without defect and perfect, is fittingly called what it is, and as it is named, so it also is. But whatever is not altogether such as it is named, that naming of it is vain and empty. And understand this as follows: if someone shows us true bread, we say:
This name is truly applied to it, and as it is called, so it also is.

But if someone should show us, in its place, something like it, fashioned by craft from the nature of stones, which has the very same shape and size, resembles it in color, and in every way displays in itself the form of the original,
yet, since it does not have the power to nourish and falls short of the nature of bread,
we say of it that it is not true bread, nor is it truly called bread, but only by extension and loose usage, and the shared name of bread is attributed to it in vain.
In the same way, everything that is not wholly what it is called bears that name by extension and loose usage. And likewise the soul has its perfection in intellect and rational speech.
And anything in which this is not present may perhaps be called a namesake of the soul, but truly a soul, never; rather, it is some vital power presented under the name of soul.

For this reason the nature of the irrational animals, as not being separated from this natural life, was likewise given for use to the authority of man by him who appointed a law for each and every one, and who ordained the eating of them in place of herbs and said:

"You shall eat all flesh as the green herb." For it is regarded as only a little higher on account of its powers of sense perception, apart from those of nourishment and growth, which belong to the green herb.

Let this be a teacher to lovers of the flesh, and let them not bind their minds to that which is in no way much higher than grasses and plants, but let them acquire zeal for gaining spiritual advancement,
in which the true soul is seen, for mere senses without understanding are possessed even by the irrational animals.

But the flow of the discourse has carried us away to another subject, for what was set before us for examination was not this, that among the things seen in human beings the power [?] of the mind is more honorable than all,
and than the materiality of bodily existence, but rather that the mind is not confined in any particular part of the members that are in us, but is equally in every part and in all of them,

neither surrounding them from outside nor being held within, in the way that casks or chains hanging from one another are seen, for these things befit certain material objects of that kind and not the mind.

But the mind's communion with the body has an ineffable and incomprehensible union: it is neither enclosed within, for the incorporeal is not enclosed in a body, nor wrapped around the outside, for the incorporeal does not wrap around anything,
nor is it encompassed; rather, in some unsearchable and inconceivable manner the mind draws near to the nature and is joined to it, and is seen with it and in it,

neither seated in it nor wrapped around it, but in a way that can be neither told nor imagined. Only this much can be said: if the nature proceeds according to its proper order, the mind too acts and governs;
but if some fault or affliction comes in, then the movement and activity of the mind also is disabled and limps in that part.
Chapter 16: Contemplation of the divine word which said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness,"

In which it is investigated what the likeness of the image is, and whether this passible and temporal creature resembles that blessed and impassible one, and how male and female are seen in the image,
which are not seen in that prototypal form. But let us go back again to that divine voice: "Let us make man in our image and likeness."
Some outsiders imagined the glory of human nature, by equating it with this world, as something small and unworthy of human glory,
for they say that man is a small world within the great one, and that, in its likeness, his being is constructed out of all the elements, and,
those who by the grandeur of the name bestow this sort of praise on human nature do not realize that they are making man savory and adorning him with the properties of the fly and the gnat.
For these too have their mixture from these four elements,

and among all beings, in each one individually, either a greater or a lesser portion of animation is seen, without which nothing subject to the senses can come into being or live. What great thing, then, is it for man's existence to be thought a figure and likeness of the world,
since heaven and earth pass away, or are changed, and all their elements pass away along with them?
But according to the teaching of the Church, what is the majesty and greatness of man?
It is this: not likeness to this created world, but being created in the image of the nature of the Creator. And perhaps you will say:
And what is the meaning of the image, or how does the bodily resemble the bodiless, and the temporal the eternal, and the shifting and changeable the unchangeable,
and the passible and corruptible the impassible and incorruptible, and this creature reared in every evil the one untouched by any evil?
For a great difference is seen between that prototypal form and what was created in its image,
for if an image has an unchanging likeness to that prototypal form, it is fittingly and truly called an image.
But if it is changed from the form set before it, it is something else and no longer its image and likeness.
So how could man, this mortal, passible and corruptible creature, be the image and likeness of that incorruptible, holy and eternal nature?

However, the true account and force of all this is truly known only to the King himself, the only Truth; but we, as far as we are able to grasp, search out the truth through some figure and parable. Thus we say concerning this question that:
Neither does the divine word lie, which said that man was created in the image of God, nor does this poor wretchedness of human nature rival or resemble that blessedness of impassible life.
And if anyone strives to equate this human worthlessness with God, he is compelled to confess one of two things: either to ascribe passibility to the Godhead,
or impassibility to humanity, so that the account of the likeness may proceed equally on both sides. But if neither is passion ascribed to the Godhead,

and neither is humanity free of passion, then without doubt there must be some other account by which we affirm the truth of the divine utterance that speaks of the creation of man in the image of God.

Now then, let us recall the divine Scripture itself; perhaps we may find in it some guidance and support for this inquiry. For when it has said, "Let us make man in image and likeness," and has said for what purpose "let us make," it adds to this statement:
"And God made man; in the image of God he made him;
male and female he made them." We have already said above that this saying was put forward to overthrow the impiety of the heretics,
so that we may learn that God made man: the Only-begotten God made him in the image of God.

And let us not divide the divinity of the Father and the Son by any notion, for the holy book has called both of them God equally: the one who made man, and the one in whose image he was made. But let us now leave off discussion of this point and turn to the inquiry before us.
And how can this be? For the divinity is blessed and humanity is wretched, and yet the book calls man in its image and likeness.
Therefore these words must be examined minutely. We find, then, that what was created in the image of God is one thing, and this present misery in which we find ourselves is another, for it says:
"God made man; in the image of God he made him." Here, then, the creation in the image of God was completed.

And after that it turns back again to the account of creation and says, "Male and female he made them." And I think that no one is so foolish as not to understand that this statement is foreign to any notion of likeness to that first-born image,
for, as the Apostle says, in Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female. But understand that by these words the text divides humanity and names it male and female,
and in this way it makes clear the twofold character of our nature,

for the constitution of our nature is double. The one part is like the divinity, according to the word of Scripture, and the other is divided by this distinction. For this is the meaning that this word of Scripture teaches us, along with its order and arrangement, for first it said
that "God made man" and that "in the image of God he made him," and then it added to these statements and said:
"Male and female he made them," which is foreign to anything that can be conceived of the divine nature.
And, as I think, by these statements divine Scripture teaches us some great and lofty doctrine.

And that doctrine is this: man stands midway between two things far removed from each other: first, the divine and incorporeal nature, and second, the irrational and brute life. And parts appropriated from both of these natures are seen in the human material and constitution:
from the divine nature, speech and intelligence, in which no division into male and female is seen; and from the brute animals, the bodily constitution and generation,
divided into male and female, for in everyone who has human life, both of these are undoubtedly seen.
But in the creation of man, as we have learned, the rational creation is older than this second order, and only afterward was this bestial communion and property of birth introduced;
for it says: "God made man in the image of God," and by these words it showed, according to the saying of the Apostle, that in such a being there was neither maleness nor femaleness;

and then it further added this property of human nature, saying: "Male and female he made them." And what is it that we learn from this? But let no one blame me for this, for I am beginning the explanation of the present matter from far back.
God by his own nature is everything good that can be conceived, and what could anyone conceive that is like him!

Rather, he is above, higher than, and surpassing every good, both conceived and inconceivable, both attainable and unattainable. And God created human life for no other reason than only for his own goodness.
And since he is such, and for this reason undertook the creation of our nature, it was not fitting that he should display the power of his goodness incompletely,
giving it some of the wealth of his good things while grudging to give others! Hence the perfect sign of his goodness is seen in this:
that is, that he both brought man from non-being into being and made him lacking in none of all good things.
But since the multitudes of his good things are many and it is impossible to enumerate them,
for this reason the word gathered everything together at once by a certain all-encompassing power of expression, when it said that man was created in the image of God.
And this saying means that he bestowed on human nature a share in all his good things, for since God is the fullness of good things,
and this being is his image, is it not then clear and evident that it too is full of every good thing, in likeness to that archetypal image?

And since the form of all good things has been created in us, along with every virtue and wisdom and whatever is seen in that archetypal form, then one of all those good things is freedom and self-determination, which is both necessary and fitting,
so that it should not be enslaved to the tyrannies of nature, but should have self-determination over its own will; for virtue is free, without a master, and acquired voluntarily,
whereas what is pressed and compelled is not called virtue, nor is it possible to call it virtue.

And in everything in which the beauty of the archetypal image is seen in the image, if there were not some difference, it would no longer be an image, nor indeed a likeness, but that very being and nature itself, entirely unchanged.
And what is that difference of the divine that is not seen in the image?
It is this: that the one is uncreated, while the other is created and constructed. And the difference of this distinction in turn brought in a train of other distinctions,

Of these things no one is ignorant; rather, it is confessed by all and evident that the uncreated nature is also unchanging and unalterable and abides always in the same state. But what is created cannot exist without change, for the very passage from non-being into being is a kind of change and alteration.
That is, it did not exist, and by the divine will it came into being. And just as the word of the Gospel calls the form stamped on a drachma the image of Caesar,

from which we learn that in its form it had a likeness to Caesar, but in the material on which it was inscribed it had a difference, so likewise is the saying now under discussion: in place of the stamped features, let us understand this word of likeness as referring to the things seen in the divine and in human nature, in which the likeness lies.
But in the material we find the difference that is seen between the uncreated and the created,
for since the one abides entirely in the same state, while the other changes and turns this way and that, as it began from alteration, for this reason,
he who knew all things before they existed, as the prophet says,
perceived by his foreknowing power in which direction the authority of the human will would incline, through its self-governing will and freedom. And since he knows the things to come,

he ordained upon the image, and contrived, this craft of division into male and female, which no longer resembles or looks toward the divine archetype, but, as I have said, is akin to the irrational nature.
But the true cause of such a craft may be known only to those who became eyewitnesses and ministers of the true Word. As for us,
as far as we are able to discover it, let us undertake the investigation of the truth by some reasoning and by likeness, and what has come to mind we do not affirm as a definitive ruling, but,
as something to be examined and as an exercise, we lay it before understanding hearers for their consideration. And what is it that we have understood? For,
when the word said that God made man, by this indefinite statement it indicated the entire constitution of humankind.

For here it did not name Adam together with the creation, as the account of creation says later on; rather, the name of the created human being is not that of a particular person but of the whole kind. And it did not say 'this one,' but those who were to be created,

those it mentioned. And by this naming of the whole nature we understand this meaning: that by the true power of foreknowledge he encompassed all human nature in that first creation. For it cannot be that in the divine creation anything should be unlimited and undetermined,
but the limit and measure and beginning and end of all beings have been ordained and measured out by the wisdom of the Creator.

Just as, if someone were building up a human body and making its color and form resemble the original, as much of its breadth and thickness and quality is needed as would complete the stature of the body and the structure of the flesh,
so too the whole fullness of humankind, built together in one body, was encompassed by the foreknowledge of God.
And this is indicated by the saying which states: "God created man; in the image of God he created him."

For the quality of being in the image does not lie in a part of the nature, nor is the divine grace confined to any one of the things seen in it; rather, his power governs every property of the race equally.

And likewise, as a sign for all: in all mind is established, and all equally have the power of forethought and understanding, and everything else by which the divine nature is uniformly portrayed in that which was created in its likeness.
Both the man who was created at the first creation of the world and the one who is to be created last of all: on all alike the divine image is depicted.

And for this reason all were given the name of one man, for to the divine power nothing is past and nothing is to come; rather, even what is awaited and what is yet to be is governed and held by that all-ruling divine power equally with what has already arrived and come to pass. Hence the whole nature to be created, from the first to the last, is one image of the uncreated nature.
But the division into male and female [?] was added to humanity afterward, for this reason, as I suppose.
Chapter 17: What must be answered to those who ask:
If procreation came in after sin, how would souls have been created,

if man had remained sinless from the beginning? But rather, before examining the matter now before us, perhaps it is better that we explain the question put forward to us by our opponents, for they say that:
Before sin neither birth is indicated, nor conception, nor any preparation for procreation.

But when they had been cast out of paradise after sin, and the bearing of children was decreed as a torment for the woman, only then did Adam know his wife, and only then did the beginning of procreation take place.
Now therefore, since there was no marriage in paradise, nor conception, nor birth, from this it must necessarily be understood

that the multiplication of souls would not have occurred if the grace of immortality had not been changed into mortality, and marriage would not be preserving the nature through those who are born, and,
in place of those who have departed, bringing in those born of it. Hence, in a certain way, the entry of sin into human life turned out to be for the better,
for the human race would have remained in the pair first made, had not the fear of death stirred the nature to provide for successors.

And again, on this matter too, the word of truth, whatever it may be, would be known only to those who, like Paul, became hearers of the ineffable mysteries of paradise and to whom their utterance was revealed; but what we understand is this:
For when the Sadducees were disputing the mystery of the resurrection, and the much-married woman,
whom those seven brothers had married, they brought forward to confirm their heresy, and they said: To which of those seven will she belong after rising from the dead?
The Lord answered them and said, not only to refute them, but to reveal to all the mystery of the resurrection and the life to come, that:

"In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, nor does death any longer have power over them, for they are equal to the angels, and they are sons of God and sons of the resurrection."
And the grace of the resurrection announces to us nothing other than the restoration of the fallen to their original state.
For that awaited holy grace of his promises us a return to that first life, and it brings those who were cast out of paradise back into it.
And since the life of those who have returned there is portrayed as proper to the angels, it is clear that the life before the transgression of the commandment was something angelic.
And truly the ascent to that first life of ours is likened to the angels, and, as has been said, there is no marriage among them.
And the hosts of the angels are countless myriads, for so Daniel has related to us in his visions.
And if no change away from the angelic order had come upon us through sin, neither would we have come to need marriage in order to multiply,
but just as there is in the nature of the angels a manner of multiplication, inexpressible and inconceivable to human minds and understanding, yet existing in any case,
so too it would have come about for man, who was made a little lower than the angels, that human nature would rise and grow to the limit determined by the will of the Creator.
But if the inquiry into the creation of souls should perplex anyone, as to how it would have been if man had not come to need the help of marriage,
let us in turn ask him about the manner of the angels' constitution: how are they countless myriads in number, and yet one in nature and essence?
And let such an answer as this suffice us against those questioners and disputers who say, "How would human beings have multiplied without marriage?" And let us say to them:
Just as the angels exist without marriage. For the restoration of man to their order makes clear his likeness to them before the transgression.

And having set this out in this way, let us go back up to our earlier discourse, namely how, after fashioning the image, the Creator crafted maleness and femaleness and introduced their division into the creature. And for this reason I think that the understanding stated above is fitting.
For he who brought everything into being, and by his own will fashioned the whole of human nature in the divine image and created it self-determining, did not wait
to see, by gradual addition, the completion of the creature by the number of souls and its rise to its fullness,
but in an instant, by his foreknowing power, he beheld the whole extent of human existence and honored it with that lofty, angelic honor.
And since by his foreseeing power he saw beforehand that the direction of its will toward the good would not be right or straight,
and that because of this it would fall from the angelic life, so that the multiplication of human souls should not be cut off,
And when they fell from the mode by which the angels multiplied and increased, for this reason, in a manner suited to its fall into sin, he prepared for our nature a form and means of increase.
And in place of that angelic incorruption, he planted in humanity this corruptible and animal succession through birth.
Therefore the great David, too, out of pity for human wretchedness, laments our nature in words such as these, saying:
"Man was in honor and did not understand." By "honor" he meant equality with the angels, and then he says:
"He imitated the senseless beasts and became like them." And truly animal is this animal birth,
which nature received through this material way of life and corruption.
Chapter 18, that the animal passions have their causes in us from kinship with the nature of the animals. And, as I suppose,
from such a beginning each of the passions, as if springing up from some fountain, spread throughout human life.
And this kinship of the passions, which is seen equally in us and in the animals, makes this statement clear.
For it is not right that the beginnings of the passions should be ascribed to human nature, which is like the divine image, on account of a condition subject to passion.
But since animal life had come into this world, man too first received something from their nature,
in accordance with the cause mentioned above, which is birth, and along with it he also received a share in the other passions present in their nature;
for it is not through anger that man becomes like God, nor is that surpassing and all-holy nature represented through lust,
or through fear and insolence and greed and hatred of inferiors, for everything of this kind is foreign to the divine image;
rather, human nature drew these passions from the animal part.
For the things by which animal life protects and guards itself, when they are transferred to human life, are changed into passions.
For anger protects the blood-eating animals, and love of lust the prolific creatures; fearfulness saves the weak, and cowardice those easily driven off by the stronger,
and gluttony the thick and fleshy; and failure to obtain what is desired becomes a cause of grief for the animals.
All this and whatever is like it came upon the constitution of human beings through this animal birth.
And grant me pardon, so that I may depict the form of the human image by means of a certain contrived comparison.
For just as is seen in those contrived sculptures, which people with leisure for such vanities fashion to cause wonder and astonishment, depicting two faces on one head,
so I see in man two opposing forms.

That is, he has a divine mind, made like the divine beauty, but his impulse toward the passions and his eagerness change his likeness and his condition toward the animals, and sometimes he becomes wholly an animal through his inclination toward animal deeds and his love of them.
And he covers the higher with the lower,
For when someone coerces the power of rational understanding, drags it into the service of the passions, and defiles deliberation and thought by slavery to the passions,
a change takes place, from that good image-likeness into the likeness of the beasts.

And he renders his whole nature corrupt in that direction, when thought, like a farmer, cultivates the beginnings of the passions, sows evil seeds, and little by little makes them grow into a great multitude.

For it pours out its own help into the power of the passions and brings up abundant fruit and an immeasurable thicket of impurity. In the same way, love of pleasure took its beginning from likeness to the beasts, but it grew through human lawlessness, and so many varieties of sinful desires were born as are not found even among the beasts.
Likewise the stirring of anger has its kinship with the wrath of the beasts, but it increases through the strengthening given by thoughts, from which are born rancor, envy, lying, deceit,
treachery, and duplicity. And all these passions are acquired through that evil working of the mind.

And if this passion of wrath were stripped of the help of thoughts and of their bitter support, it would be weak and powerless, and like bubbles of water it would quickly swell up, at once subside, and vanish.
Thus the gluttony of swine introduced greed, and the friskiness of the horse became the beginning of pride.

And each and every cause arising from the irrationality of the beasts has been changed into wickedness by that evil use of the mind. So too the reverse happens: if thought changes the firmness of such impulses, each of them is changed into virtue.
For anger produces courage, timidity produces caution, fear produces obedience, hatred produces turning away from evil, and the power of love produces desire for the true good;
and high-spiritedness of mind lifts one above the passions and keeps reason unenslaved by all evils.
The Apostle too praises the form of such elevation and repeatedly commands us to think on heavenly things. And thus it is possible to find
that every such impulse, when raised up together with the elevation of the mind, becomes conformed to the beauty of the divine image.
But since the downward pull of sin is heavy and drags things down, it becomes greater than the other,
and by the weight of the bestial nature it drags down the ruling mind of the soul, more than the elevation of the mind lifts up what is earthly.

Hence our wretchedness often becomes unaware of the divine gifts, and, like a squalid and ugly mask, covers the beauty of the image with the passion of the flesh. For this reason those people may be considered somewhat excusable
who look upon such an image and are convinced that the divine image-likeness is not seen in these people.

But it should not be so; rather, the divine image should be examined in those people who have directed their lives well. For if some passionate and flesh-loving person makes one disbelieve that man is adorned with divine beauty, then undoubtedly,
Surely someone lofty in virtue and purified of the passions will confirm for you that higher part of human beauty.
And it is better that you understand this statement through an illustration: someone notorious among the wicked, that is, Jeconiah,
or some other imitator of his, corrupted the beauty of nature with the defilement of wickedness; but by Moses and those who imitated him the beauty of the image was kept spotless and pure.

And among those in whom the beauty was not corrupted, among them shines the credibility of these sayings, that man was created in the image of God. But who knows, perhaps someone may be ashamed of this life of ours, sustained by food and constituted like that of the beasts, and may therefore think the creation of man unworthy of the image of God. Rather, let him hope,
for nature will at some time be freed even from this service in the life to come, as the Apostle says: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink."
And the Lord declared: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes out of the mouth of God."
And the mystery of the resurrection makes our life equal to that of the angels. And since there is no eating among the angels, it is sufficient ground for believing that man too, who is to live,
like the angels, will be freed from such service.

Chapter 19. To those who say that the enjoyment of the good things we await will again consist in eating and drinking, since it is written that in the beginning the life of human beings in paradise consisted in these things. But perhaps someone may say that Scripture does not speak of man's return as being to the same form of life,
since that first life consisted in eating, whereas afterward we shall be freed from such service. But I,
as I hear from the holy Scriptures, have not learned of bodily eating only, nor of joy derived from the flesh alone,
but I know also another kind of nourishment, resembling the nourishment of the body, whose delight rises to the rational soul alone, concerning which Wisdom commands the hungry:
"Eat my bread," and the Lord calls blessed those who hunger for such eating, and again says:
"Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink," and the great Isaiah commands the mighty of the earth to drink joy, which is the understanding of those divine teachings.

And again there is also a prophetic saying about those deserving of punishment, that they should be condemned as if by famine. But the famine is not a lack of any bread or of water, but a deficiency of the word; for it says:
"I do not speak of a famine of bread, nor of a thirst for water, but of a famine of hearing the words of God."
So also of that paradise of God, which he planted in Eden.

And Eden is translated as "delight." A worthy understanding must be held of its fruits and of the nourishment of man from them, without doubting, and one must not imagine this food that flows away and passes out of the body in the life of paradise. For it says: "Of every tree of the garden you shall surely eat."
Who, then, would give wholly to the hungry man that tree of paradise in which all good things are enclosed, the one that is named "all," whose delight the divine law makes man share?
For by a perfect and firm word it holds every form of good united in itself, and all of it is one.
And again, who will deliver me from tasting that mixed and twofold tree?
And is it not indeed known to those who have understanding what that "all" is whose fruit is life, and again what this mixed thing is whose end is death? For
he who ungrudgingly set before man the enjoyment of "all" kept him, by a certain power and dispensation, from partaking of that mixed thing.
And, as I think, the great David and the wise Solomon interpret this figure,
for they show that the grace of that permitted food is one and the same: it is in truth the true good and is called the all-good. For David says:
"Delight in the Lord." And Solomon gives to wisdom itself, which is the Lord, the name "tree of life," and both are one.
That is, the tree of life and that "every" tree, the eating of which the word commands to man, who was created in the image of God.
But set in opposition to that tree is another tree, the eating of which is knowledge of good and evil.
It does not bear each of these fruits separately and apart, as is indicated, but bears fruit mixed and blended, mingled from contrary richnesses. From eating it the guide of life holds man back,

but the serpent urges the eating, so as to open the door to death. And when he urged it, he became persuasive, for he anointed that fruit with a certain beauty and desire, so that it would appear desirable and would stir man by longing to taste it.
Chapter 20: What the life of paradise was, and what the forbidden tree was, and how the name of the tree of knowledge ought to be understood. What, then, is that tree
which has the knowledge of good and evil blended together and blossoms with the desire of the senses? What is it?

Perhaps I shall not be thinking outside the truth if I take the meaning of "knowing" as the starting point and indication for our inquiry? For, as I think, in this place Scripture does not give the name "knowledge" to skill
or to intelligence, for in the usage of the Scriptures I find other distinctions for judgment and understanding.
For the Apostle lays down that skillfully distinguishing good and evil is the work of full maturity, and he calls it the training of the senses.
For this reason he also commands the testing of all things and assigns judging to those who are spiritual.

But "knowledge" does not everywhere indicate skill and science, in keeping with the word as it is indicated here, but rather the disposition toward those who are one's own, and choice. As it says: "The Lord knows those who are his own," and he says to Moses, "I know you more than all."
But concerning those given over to evil, he who knows all things says: "I do not know you." Hence this tree,
That from which mixed knowledge is brought forth as fruit is among the forbidden things, and its fruit is mixed from opposing qualities, and it has the serpent as its helper and praiser.
And understand it this way: evil does not lie there naked, nor does it appear according to its own nature, as it really is.
For if that were so, it would surely be ineffective, since nothing good would flatter it and draw the deceived person to desire it.
But as it is, the nature of evil is something mixed and blended, and it keeps what destroys and ruins hidden in its depth, like a snare.

And by a visible deception it displays a semblance [?] of something good. Lovers of silver think the colorful appearance of that material is good, and yet the love of silver has been called the root of all evils. Or who would fall into the stinking mire of fornication,
if desire did not make it appear good and desirable to the one dragged along by that lure [?] of its?
In the same way the remaining sins also keep their corruptions hidden, and at first perception they come to be thought desirable by the unwary through some deception, and are reckoned good.
And since most people reckon as good whatever delights the senses, and there is a certain sharing of name between good and evil,

between the apparent and the true, for this reason the desire formed toward evil, as if toward good, was called by Scripture the knowledge of good and evil. And thus it interprets that knowledge as something blended through a certain joint attestation and mixture,
neither as unmixed evil, for it blossoms with something good, nor as pure good, for it is shrouded in evil,
but it says that the fruit of the forbidden tree is mixed of both sides, and calls it a bringer of death to those who taste it, and it openly cries out that:

The true good is simple and straightforward by nature, and foreign to all duplicity and to any joining with its opposite, whereas evil is many-colored and takes on all kinds of forms, and it is thought to be one thing and found by experience to be another.
The knowledge of it, that is, discerning it by experience, becomes the beginning and cause of death and corruption.

And for this reason the serpent showed the evil fruit of sin, yet it did not show it openly as its nature really was, for the man would not have been led astray by manifest evil. Rather, it adorned what it displayed with a certain beauty, and made the tasting of it felt through a certain desire of the senses, and in this way its trickery [?] appeared credible to the woman, as Scripture says:
And the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasing to the eyes to look at and beautiful to contemplate.
And she took and ate. And that eating became the mother of death for human beings.
And this is the mixed fruitfulness whose force the text plainly interprets, whence the tree was given the name knowledge of good and evil.
For, like a deadly poison mixed with honey, it is thought good because of the taste that sweetens the senses, but because it destroys the one who touches it, it becomes more evil than all evil.
And since that evil and deadly poison had been mingled into human life,

From the time when man, that great thing and name, that image of the divine nature, became like vanity, according to the word of the prophet, it follows that whatever good and better thing is seen or conceived among us is all to be assigned to the honor of being in the image,
but whatever is distressing and whatever wretchedness is mixed into our life is alien to and far from the divine likeness.
Chapter 21: That the resurrection is not credible only from the proclamation of the Scriptures,

but rather the hope of it is confirmed from the order and sequence of things. Yet evil is not so strong as to prevail over the good that comes from God, nor is the error of our nature higher and firmer than the divine wisdom,
for neither is it possible for what is turning and changeable to be firmer and more unchangeable than what remains forever in one state and is firm and unchangeable in good things,
since the divine purpose is unchangeable and unmoved in everything and in every respect. But the mutability of our nature does not stand firm even in evil.
For that which is always changing, if its course is toward the good, never ceases from advancing forward, since this matter of progress in the good is boundless,
for it finds no end of what it seeks,

which it might grasp and so cease from advancing. But if it turns its inclination toward the opposite side, then, once it has completed that course of evil and has reached the summit of the measure of evils, from then on the direction of its course becomes motionless,

since it finds from nature no means of standing still, and, having run through that course of evil by compulsion, it turns its course toward the good. For evil does not advance beyond its limits, but is brought to completion by involuntary ends, and so,
the sequel of the good is fittingly joined to that end of evil,
and so that movement of our nature turns back again toward the course of the good, made wise by the memory of its failures, so that it may not fall again into the same evils.
And since by such compelled endings the nature of evil is contained and bounded, it is beyond doubt that our turning back toward the good will take place again,

just as the wise men of the world, the investigators of lofty matters, say that the nature of light is more extensive and fills the whole world, whereas darkness comes in through the division made by the shadows of the earth. And this comes about because of the spherical body, when its roundness blocks the brilliance of the sun on its far side.
But the sun is much vaster than the earth in size,

and when its light spreads on every side around the sphere of the earth, then, as its rays pass beyond it on every side, their tips come together again with one another. And if there were some means by which the sun could pass beyond the measure of that roundness
through which the shadow comes in, there would without doubt be everlasting light, uninterrupted by darkness.
Understand it the same way concerning us as well: for when we pass beyond the boundary of evil and reach the end of the shadows of sin,

Let us again receive manifold light and live in the light; and by as much as the nature of good is broader than the measure of evil, by so much the more good things will God Almighty have graciously granted us:

again paradise, and again the tree of life, and again the grace of the image, and the honor of dominion. For that future state will not be like all the things that are now seen in this world and have been granted by God to human beings,

but that kingdom and the hope of delight are something else, which cannot be expressed in words, is unfathomable to the mind and cannot be conceived by the heart. But let us return to our earlier discourse.
Chapter 22. To those who say: Since the resurrection is good and desirable, why has it not already happened, but will instead take place after certain revolutions of time?
And perhaps someone may become winged in mind toward that sweet hope, and may count it a burden and a hardship that those good things do not come quickly,
which are higher than human mind and understanding, and in his longing the prolongation of these intervening times may seem grievous to him.
But let him not be fainthearted like infants, who, if a delay occurs in the fulfillment of their desire, even for a short time, take it hard, are vexed and fret.
For since all things are governed by wisdom and reason, it is necessary and unavoidable that he should consider no matter to be without a share in the governance of that very Wisdom and Word.
Therefore do not say: What is this matter? And why does the passage from this hard life to that desired blessedness not happen immediately, but with certain appointed times
this heavy and fleshly worldly course is prolonged and awaits the end of the consummation of all things,
so that only then the human race may be set free, as if from reins, and at that point ascend to that incorruptible and ageless life?
To such words, then, we say this; and whether our word comes near the truth, Truth itself knows.
I repeat the earlier statement, namely: "God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness.
And God made man; in the image of God he made him." The likeness of God, which is seen in all human nature, received its completion,
but Adam had not yet been made; for the name Adam, translated from the Hebrew language, means one formed from earth,
as the Apostle says, who, being trained beyond all others, knew well the force of his ancestral language, and when he rendered it into Greek, called Adam earthy and made of clay.
So man was made in the image of God, that is, all human nature; and he was made by that almighty Wisdom. Hence, not a part of the whole,
but the entire fullness of human nature was seen in an instant by the one who holds all the ends of the earth, as it is written: "In his hand are all the ends of the earth."

He who knows all things before their creation saw and perceived how great a number the whole fullness of humanity would reach. And since he truly knew our turning toward evil, and that our being would fall of its own will from the honor of the angels and would take on a share of contempt and lowliness, he therefore also mingled something from the nature of the irrational animals into his own image,
for indeed in that divine and blessed nature there is no division into male and female,

but he took this property and characteristic for man from the constitution of the irrational animals. For it was not in the exalted order of our creation that God brought forth the multiplication of tribes and kindreds, nor yet when he created [man] in his own image
did he then give humans the power of increase and multiplication; but when he had separated them by division into male and female, only then did he say:
"Increase and multiply and fill the earth." For such a thing was not a property of the divine nature,
but of the irrational animals, as Genesis says, for God first gave this command to the animals.

For if, before the division into male and female, such a power of increase had been added to human nature by that divine command, we would not have come to need this manner of birth by which the irrational animals are born.

So by his foreknowing power he foresaw this fullness of humanity, those who were to enter this life through that animal birth, which God arranges in a certain order and harmony of all things. And since such a manner of birth,
which came upon humans, made necessary the naming of our lowly nature as male and female, which he foresaw before creation, he who sees things to come as equal to what has already happened,
he therefore ordained times matched to the making of humans, so that, when those predetermined souls have been born,
the extent of the times may also be completed, and only then is this river-like flow of times to come to rest, when a human being no longer springs up in them,
and when the birth of humans has come to an end, the times too shall cease along with their ending, and only then shall the restoration of all things take place,
and with that change of all things humanity too shall be changed from corruption and mortality to incorruption and immortality.

And the great apostle understood this very matter and wrote of it beforehand in the epistle to the Corinthians, and he foretold that sudden cessation of the times and the reverse change of all things, where he says:
"Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall not all fall asleep, but we shall all be renewed in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at that last trumpet,"
for at the end of human nature, when that foreknown measure of the times reaches completion, and the number of souls no longer lacks the addition of even one soul,
at once that change and renewal of beings shall take place, which, because of the indivisibility and inseparability of the time, he called an instant and the twinkling of an eye,
When the times have reached the summit of time and nothing remains unaccomplished of the things that were appointed, as soon as the trumpet of the resurrection sounds, which awakens the dead,
those too who are left in this life, like those risen from the dead, will be renewed and in an instant changed into incorruption,

and this weight of the flesh will no longer drag them down, nor the density of the earth, but they will be caught up upon the air, as it is written: "We shall be caught up upon the air to meet the Lord, and so we shall be with the Lord forever."
Now therefore let us wait for that appointed and inescapable time, which grows and is extended along with the increase of humankind; for indeed the patriarchs too,
who lived in the times of Abraham, longed to see those good things and sought the heavenly fatherland, as the Apostle says,
yet they have in hope the joy of the good things that are awaited, for God foresaw something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us.
And if they endure the delay and the time, they who only by faith and hope saw those good things from afar and greeted them,

and have treasured up by faith the certainty of the delights they await, in the truthfulness of him who promised, what is fitting for most of us, who because of our deeds do not even have hope of what is better!
The soul of the prophet too fainted with longing, and he testifies to it, for he says: "My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord," even if it should be only to be cast aside there,
which he has reckoned greater and higher than some distinguished dwellings of sinners in this life.
Yet he nevertheless endured such a time, although he called that dwelling there blessed and held even a small portion of it more precious than a thousand years, and said:
"One day in your courts is better than thousands."
Yet he was not displeased by that inescapable ordering of created things, and he declared that even waiting in hope for good things is sufficient blessedness for human beings, and he sang:
"Blessed is the man who hopes in the Lord."
Therefore we too ought not to be distressed over this short time of hope, but ought to be diligent about this: that we not fall away from the good things that are awaited.
It is just as if someone were to tell an inexperienced person that at harvest time there will be a gathering of fruits,
and the storehouses will be filled and the tables will overflow with good things in that time of plenty; it would then be vain and idle for anyone to try to hasten the coming of that time,
for seed must be sown, and fruitfulness must be prepared through labor and effort, while that time, whether one wishes it or not, will without doubt come in its own season.

But they will not look upon it alike, the one who prepared plenty of fruits for himself beforehand and the one who is left at that time destitute of all preparation. So likewise there must be full assurance concerning that time, which has been made known to all by the divine proclamations,
and that the time of renewal will come without doubt, and we are not to search out the times, for it has been said:
"It is not for you to know the times and years, nor to stir up any thoughts by which the soul might be weakened [?] in its hope of the resurrection,
but to be strengthened by faith through those good things that are awaited, and by a spotless way of life to trade for and purchase the delights that are to come.

Chapter 23: That whoever acknowledges a beginning of the creation of the world must without doubt acknowledge an end as well. But if anyone should contemplate the present course of this world, and see its orderly and harmonious extension through time, and say that it is neither right nor possible, as was foretold, for this revolution to cease and this motion to stop, it is clear that such a person
does not believe that heaven and earth were created by God in the beginning either,
for whoever grants a beginning to motion will certainly have no doubt about an end either, and whoever does not accept an end will not admit a beginning either.
But just as we believe that the ages were established by the word of God, according to the saying of the apostle, and that what is seen was not made from what is manifest,
let us hold the same faith toward the word of God, who has unquestionably foretold the cessation of existing things and made it necessary.

But as to how this will happen, let us entirely root that out from our inquiry. For there too we accepted by faith that visible things were established from things not visible, and we passed over the investigation of what is incomprehensible, even though reason set before us many questions to investigate and gave no small grounds for disputing what is believed.
For there too it was possible, by those reasonings drawn from what commonly happens, to pervert the faith,

and to hold that the account of the creation of matter is not true, which Holy Scripture proclaims when it establishes that all created things were created by God and came into being. This is what those who heretically dispute the word do: they say that matter is without beginning together with God, and they put forward such treacherous arguments as these:
that since God is by nature simple and immaterial, without measure, without limit, and uncompounded, and foreign to circumscription by forms,
whereas all matter is encompassed and perceived through distance and measure, and does not escape the grasp of the senses,
and by color and shape and size and quality and harshness and resistance and the remaining properties that are seen in it

it becomes known, none of which can be perceived in the divine nature; how then was the visible born from the immaterial, and how was divided and extended matter born from what is without distance and undivided?
For if we are to believe that this was with him, it is clear that it was in him in some ineffable manner, and that afterward it came forth and was born from him.
But if materiality was with him, how did the immaterial one have matter within him?
And likewise, in the same way, with everything else by which material nature is characterized. And if quality is with God, how is God without quality?
And if composition is seen in him, how is he simple and undivided and uncompounded?
Thus reason would indeed be compelled to reckon him as material, because of the composition of matter from him.
And perhaps, if in some way they should flee from this, they would be forced to devise matter brought in from outside for his preparation of all things.
And if it was outside God, then it was certainly something other than God, counted together with the Unbegotten in eternity; hence two unbegotten and beginningless things,
equal to one another, would have to be set forth by the argument: the one working by art, and the other receiving his art into itself.

Now therefore, if someone under such a compulsion should count matter as co-beginningless with the Creator of all, the Manichaeans would find great support for their blasphemies, they who make the cause of materiality equal in unbegottenness to the good nature.
But we hear from Scripture that all things were created by God, and we believe it; and as to how they were with God,
since this is beyond our reasoning, we do not undertake to investigate, for we believe that the divine power is able to do all things:
both to create what does not exist, and to give quality and richness to what has come into being,

as it may will. Hence, as is fitting, we attribute the creation of beings from non-being to the divine power, and we hold this sufficient in place of everything; and likewise the restoration of all things
we ascribe to that same power, and we devise nothing else beyond this faith,

although it would have been possible to refute more fully those vain thinkers and disputers concerning matter, and to persuade them by a multitude of arguments [?], so that we might not be thought to be speakers of idle and empty words.

Chapter 24. A reply to those who say that matter is co-beginningless with God. For truly the divine preaching is not in error when it proclaims the creation of matter by the immaterial and incorporeal God,

for we find all matter composed of certain richnesses and qualities; if it were stripped of these in itself, it would no longer be graspable by reason, and every form of quality and richness is separated by reason from that which underlies it, or else is depicted [?].
But a rational account is invisible and not something seen bodily,

and suppose some animal or piece of wood were lying before us to be viewed, or some other substance prepared from material things. We then conceive many distinctions in what lies before us, the account of each of which remains unmixed with the things with which it is seen joined,

for the account of colour is one thing, and that of weight and quality another, and again that of extent and of the distinctive property perceived by touch; likewise that of softness and tenderness and of being two cubits long, and of the remaining things mentioned in material objects, which are not like one another, neither in substance nor in bodily composition,

for the account that interprets them presents each of them separately, just as it is, and in this way the definition of each of them is understood, and they share in nothing else with those richnesses of quality that underlie them.
Now therefore, since colour is invisible, and likewise kind and quality and quantity and the other such properties,

But if each of them is separated from the matter that underlies them, the whole principle of the body is dissolved. And since this is so, it is surely fitting that, just as we find the separation of these things to be the cause of the body's dissolution, so we should understand their coming together to be what begets material nature.
For just as there is no body that does not have color and shape and kind and measure and weight and the other properties;

and each of these is not a body, but something else, distinct and apart from the body. So likewise, conversely, wherever these aforementioned things come together, they produce the bodily subsistence, and yet the contemplation of these properties in themselves is immaterial.
And the nature of the Godhead is incorporeal and invisible.
Do you see, then, that it is not incongruous for the bodily constitution to be fashioned by the incorporeal nature from these invisible causes?
So that the incorporeal nature might bring forth invisible powers, and their coming together in turn might unite this material nature, create it, and bring it into being?
These arguments, then, we have set forth as external ones, but may we not be separated from the faith,

by which we have been assured that all things were brought from non-being into being by God, and likewise of the renewal and restoration of beings, about which we have no doubt, as we have learned from Scripture.
Chapter 25. How one of those outside may be persuaded by the teaching of Scripture concerning the resurrection. But perhaps someone, these dissolved bodies
may look upon, and may measure the divine might by the strength of his own weakness, and may call the mystery of the resurrection unbelievable,
and may hold it impossible that these things now moving should come to rest and that those motionless should rise. But to such a person,

let the trustworthy testimony and truthfulness of our preacher be set before him as a great sign and miracle of the truth of the resurrection; and as a means of persuasion concerning what he said, let the fulfillment of the other things he foretold suffice as confirmation.
And since divine Scripture has set before us many and varied sayings, it is possible, by examining those other sayings, also to examine the mystery of the resurrection,
whether it is true or false. For if error and falsehood are exposed in the others, this one too will undoubtedly not remain free of falsehood.
But if it has the truth as witness in all the others, it would surely be fitting on their account to believe also in the truth of the foretelling of the resurrection.

Now, then, let us recall one or two of the things foretold, and compare with them the correspondence of their fulfillment, so that we may learn from them whether this word about the resurrection is true.

For who would not know how the community of the Israelites flourished in the beginning, and had power equal to the whole world, and what their kingdom in Jerusalem was like, and how great the walls and what manner of towers,
and also the magnificence of the Temple,
which seemed worthy of wonder even to the Lord's disciples, so that they implored the Lord to look at it and were astonished at the sight, as the Gospel says, and they said to him:
"Look, behold what stones and what buildings are seen here!" But the Lord foretold to them the desolation that was to come and declared:
After a little while nothing of them will remain.
And likewise, at the time of the Passion, when the women were lamenting for him and mourning over the unjust sentence against him, since they could not perceive the power of the divine dispensation,
he himself commanded them to cease lamenting for him, since the matter was not worthy of lament, but to keep that mourning and weeping for the time that is truly worthy of weeping,
when the city would be surrounded by warriors, and the affliction would grow so severe that even the unborn would be called blessed,
when he foretold the defilement of eating their own children and said: They will call blessed the wombs that did not bear [?] and did not rear.
Now then, where is their kingdom, and the temple and the walls, and the pinnacles of the towers? Or where is that might of the Israelites?
Are they not scattered, one here and another there, over almost the whole world, and through their desolation was not their kingdom also laid waste?
And, as I suppose, the Lord foretold this and such things beforehand, yet that prophecy of the Savior was not for the sake of those events themselves,

for what would the foretelling of what was certainly to come have profited them? They would surely have known it without doubt from experience, even if they had not heard of what was to be. Rather, it was so that through these things they might learn faith in higher matters, and because the testimony of events in these matters made the truth of those other matters credible as well.
For just as, if some farmer were to declare the power of certain seeds, and some people inexperienced in farming were to disbelieve him,
one of the seeds would be enough as testimony to that farmer's truthfulness, as surety for the full measure of seeds,
for whoever had seen one grain of wheat or barley, or of any kind of seed, lying in the measure,
after it had been sown in tilled ground and had come up as an ear, would thereafter, because of that one, no longer be unbelieving about the others.

In the same way, understand also concerning the mystery of the resurrection; for the experience of his own resurrection is enough, together with these things that were said, as testimony to the truth,
which we learned not by word but by deed, for,

since the wonder of the resurrection was great and beyond being believed, he began with lesser wonders to make the resurrection of the dead credible, and little by little he strengthened our faith and accustomed it with gentleness,
as a mother feeds an infant step by step, and while it is still tender and has a mouth like water, gives it milk to suck from the breast,
and after its teeth have come up, she nourishes it with bread that is not whole [?],
but chewed, so that the infant's tender and unaccustomed gums may not be wounded,
and then, according to the growth [?] of its age and strength, she leads it up from infant foods to taking solid nourishment,
so in like manner the Lord fed and reared human faintheartedness, as if it were some immature infant, by means of wonders,
for first, through those given up as lost to sickness, he began to show the beginning of the resurrection, something truly great and lofty,
yet not so great as to be thought incredible, for he rebuked the fever that was burning Peter's mother-in-law, and so mighty was the power of his authority and the departure of the pain from her,
so that she rose and served those who were there, she who had reached the gates of death.
And then he increased the height of his power still further: the son of the royal official, who had all but come to perishing, as the Gospel testifies,
that he was about to die and that his father was crying out,

saying, "Come before the child dies" — such a one, given up for lost, he raised up at once. And he made his power more wondrous still, for while he had not yet drawn near, he sent him salvation from afar. And so again, step by step, he went up to higher wonders.
And when he was going to raise the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, he cleansed the woman with the flow of blood and made public what had been hidden,
and by going slowly he gave death time. And when the soul had separated from the body, he calmed the wailing and lamentation of those who were in turmoil and weeping for her,
and by a command he raised the girl as if from sleep, brought the dead one to life, and lifted human weakness to a higher measure.
And then he raised the wonder higher again, and by greater powers made a way for people to faith in the resurrection,
when in the city of Nain he raised the son of the widow, no longer a child
but a youth who was coming to full manhood, about whom the Gospel tells us a little out of much,
for it says that his mother was a widow. Do you see the heaviness of the calamity?
For she no longer had any hope of bearing children by which she might heal the affliction of her loss,

and she had no other in place of the dead one to look to, for he was her only-begotten. And how great an evil this was, no one is ignorant who is not a stranger to nature, for for him alone she had undergone the pains of childbirth,
and him alone she had reared at her breasts, and he alone brightened her table, and he alone was the adornment of her house with his play, his eagerness, his obedience,
his splendid going about in the streets, in the exercise grounds among the gathering of youths, and everything else that was sweet and desirable to a mother's eyes,
having only just reached the time of marriage, the shoot of the family, the branch of the inheritance, the staff of old age. And again, the addition of his age becomes the cause of further grief;

for in calling him a youth, it indicated the flower of his withered beauty: the sprouting of the thickness of his beard, the luxuriant growth of his hair and forelocks [?], and the colour of his cheeks and temples.
And how must his mother's heart have been over him,

or with what furnace would her bowels not have burned, and with what wailing would she not have wasted herself, when she saw such a one fallen before her like a lifeless carcass, so that her great wailings would not even let the crowd bury him!
When the Lord saw this, he had compassion and touched the bier, and those who were carrying it stood still before him, and he said to the dead man:
"Young man, I say to you, arise," and immediately he rose, and he gave him alive to his mother. And while he had not yet been brought to the grave, the Lord performed this wonder,
in which the command was equal to the former one, but the wonder was greater, so that this visible act might make credible that resurrection which is hard to believe.
Again, a certain Lazarus, a friend of the Lord, fell ill, and the Lord did not go to see him, so that death might find its opportunity and snatch him away from life.
So the Lord told the disciples, in Galilee, of the illness and death of Lazarus,
and although the disciples were reluctant, for fear of the Jews, to go up to Judea again, yet the authority of the Lord prevailed over their will,
and they came up to Bethany, so that the common resurrection of all might be made known to them and to the whole world,
and they arrived there four days before the passion of the Lord,
when every funeral rite had already been completed for him and he had spent four days in the tomb,
so that he was already close to stinking and decomposing.
Then indeed he displayed in divine splendor, by a loftier marvel, that unbelievable mystery of the resurrection of all,
for he no longer raised someone up from illness, nor brought back to life one close to death, nor made alive a child who had only just died, nor raised from the bier a youth being carried to burial,
but a grown man, buried four days, stinking and decomposed, so that even his sisters did not think it proper for the Lord to approach, because of the foulness

that had resulted from the dissolution and stench of their brother in the tomb. But the Lord made him alive with a single call, and made the resurrection of all credible. And this is that through which we await the common resurrection, which we have learned from successive experience. As the apostle says concerning the resurrection of all:
The Lord will descend with a command and with the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet of God, and will raise the dead incorruptible,

so too now the man who was in the tomb cast off death like sleep at that voice and command of the Lord, and shook off the corruption of death that had come upon him as if it were dust, and came out of the tomb at a run, whole and unharmed. Nor was he even hindered from coming out by the bonds and wrappings with which his hands and feet were bound.
Is this then too small a thing to make the resurrection of the dead credible? Or do you seek to be assured by other deeds still greater than these?
And, as I think, it was not in vain that the saying was spoken at Capernaum by the Lord, as if from the mouth of men,

which he said about himself: "Surely you will say this parable to me: Physician, heal yourself." For it was fitting that he, who through other bodies had shown people the marvel of the resurrection, should confirm the word of the resurrection through his own person as well. See the power of the preaching fulfilled in others, that is, in those who were about to die, and in the child who had died at that very moment,
and in the one who was being carried to burial, and in the dead man who stank and had decomposed, for he gave life to all of them by the same command.
And you seek also the resurrection of one who went down to death through wounds and the shedding of blood, lest the grace of that life-giving power should somehow be impaired in this?
See the hands pierced by nails. See the side opened by a spear.
Bring your fingers to the print of the nails. Examine with your hand the wound of the spear. Do you not perceive how wide the breadth of the spear was, and to what depth that wound and gash reached?

For if the opening of the wound admitted a human hand, what need is there to state how deep it went! Now therefore, since this one truly rose from the dead, as heaven and earth and all angels and men testify, is it not time to say that apostolic word:
"How do some say that there is no resurrection of the dead?"
And since everything foretold by the Lord shows its truth through actual events, which we have learned not only from words but rather from events and from those very people themselves
who rose and came back to life, and since the truth of all this, and the miracles and signs, shine brighter than the light of the sun, what ground for unbelief still remains?
Shall we not part from and scatter like chaff the empty and vainly reasoning error of the pagan philosophers, and instead embrace and hold fast the simple and guileless faith?
For we have learned from the prophet the pattern of grace, since he says: "You take away their spirit from them, and they fail and return to their own earth.
You send forth your spirit and they are created, and you renew the face of the earth,"
at the point where he also speaks of the Lord's joy over his works, when sinners have vanished from the earth.
For how could sin still have a name at that time, when sin no longer exists?
Chapter 26. That the mystery of the resurrection is not unfitting. But there are some
who, through the weakness of human reasonings, measure divine power by our own standard, and what is beyond our grasp they say is not possible for God either.
For they put before us the disappearance of those long dead, and of those whose bones were consumed by fire and turned to dust and ash,

and along with this they bring up carnivorous beasts, and flesh swallowed by fish and its union with their own flesh, and its being eaten in turn by men, and its changing through digestion into the bulk of human flesh,
and they put forward many other such worthless and contemptible arguments, unworthy of the power and authority of the great God, in order to overthrow the divine teaching,
as though God were unable, by a return along the same paths, to give back to man the matter and substance of his own constitution.
But we shall cut short the long windings of their much talk with a brief word,

for we acknowledge the dissolution of bodies and their return to that from which they were created, and not only the return of earth to earth, according to the divine decree, but also to air and water.
And since all our elements and structures join with their own kindred elements, from which they were built up, then whether human flesh is mingled with carnivorous birds,
or with savage beasts, or enters the teeth of fish, or is consumed by fire into dust and ash and smoke,

And in whatever direction one may imagine the disappearance of human bodies, they are without doubt within the world and have not been snatched away from the earth. For we have learned from the divine books that the ends of the earth are held and governed by the hands of God.
And if you are not ignorant of anything that is in your own hands, how can you think that the might of God and his knowledge are weaker than your power,
his knowledge, which searches out all things, and that it could not find out with precision what he contains in those boundless spans and holds in those all-ruling palms?
Chapter ႩႪ [?]. That it is possible for human bodies, scattered among all the elements, to be gathered back together from all of them, each into each individual person. But who knows,
perhaps you look to the constitution of all these elements and think it impossible for these elements that are in us, once scattered into the air and united with the property of their own elements,
that is, the hot and the moist and the dry and the cold, to be separated again from what is common and to return to their own bodies.
And do you not understand from human customs that not even this exceeds the bounds of divine power?
For surely you have seen in human life herds gathered in common, or droves of animals grazing together.
Yet when they are divided up to their owners, whether by habit and affection or by a mark, each of them returns to its own possessor.
And if you understand the same about yourself as well, you will not stray from what is fitting,
for the soul has a certain natural love toward the body in which it dwelt, and a hidden knowledge and love of this constitution here is stamped by nature upon the soul, like a mark and a sign.
And thus that commonness remains unconfused, even though it has been divided into what is distinct.

And since this is so, and the soul in turn draws its own proper elements to itself by itself, what labor, tell me, would it be for the divine power not to hinder its own things from being gathered together, when by some ineffable attraction of nature they are drawn to what is proper to them? For this,
that some sign of our constitution remains upon the soul even after dissolution, is made clear by the conversation in hell of those whose bodies had decayed in the grave.
For some mark of the form of the body had remained upon the soul, by which Lazarus was recognized.
And the rich man was not unknown either. Therefore it is neither strange nor unfitting to believe this: that to the bodies rising again from these common elements their own elements should return.
And moreover, if one examines our nature closely, our constitution is not wholly dissolved and made to vanish,
for it would be altogether incomprehensible and unknowable if it had no stability at all from nature. But as it is, one part of us remains fixed, and another advances through change,
for the body is changed by growth and diminution and, like a garment, is clothed in the successive ages one after another,

But form and kind remain unchanged through all changes. Once they have been stamped upon the constitution, they are not stripped of the marks of nature, but through all the changes of the body they remain unchanged in their own marks.
And understand it this way: if you strip away the alteration caused by affliction, which comes over the form like some alien face,

with which the form is clothed through the ugliness of disease, and if this is stripped off by the word, as with Naaman the Syrian, or as with those lepers mentioned in the Gospel, then the form hidden by the affliction appears again through its own marks and becomes recognizable.
But the divine image-likeness of the soul is not imprinted on this corruptible and changeable constitution, but on that which is eternal and always remains the same.
And since the conditions that distinguish forms are shaped by the changes of the constitution, and the constitution is nothing other than a mixture of elements,
and by elements we mean all those elements that complete the constitution, of which the human body too is built, and the form of these remains upon the soul like some seal and carved likeness,
then even if that form is effaced, the seal inscribed upon it

is not lost from its mind, nor does it become unrecognized. Rather, at the time when the elements are restored, it receives into itself the same form, whichever fits that first carving; and without doubt that will fit which was stamped by the form from the beginning.
And for this reason we say that nothing strange or unfitting happens when each individual body takes its own elements out of the common elements and is restored to its own constitution.

It is as they say of quicksilver: if it is poured out of the vessel in which it stood onto some flat and dusty place, it breaks up into tiny pieces and scatters among the dust, yet it does not mix with any of the dust or earth at all.

And if someone gathers together again what was scattered, nothing at all of the dust and earth clings to it, but it remains in the same purity it had at first. Understand the same about the human constitution and mixture also.
If only the divine command is given,
of their own accord and in an instant, the individual elements and parts are molded to one another and blend with each other.

And no labor at all befalls the one who unites the natures by this. For among the plants of the earth too we see no hardship or labor of nature in wheat or barley or millet, or in any other sown or unsown plants, changing into stalk and awn and ear.
For each seed of its own accord, without hardship, changes and grows according to its own constitution.
Now then, if one water nourishes all plants, and all those nourished by it draw moisture in keeping with their own constitution and bring their own constitution to completion, what wonder is it
if the same thing also happens at the resurrection of the dead, and each body, according to the form of its seed, receives its own constitution by the will of God!

Hence from all this it can be known that nothing foreign to experience is found in the preaching of the resurrection, even though we have passed over in silence what is most credible and knowable from our own nature, that is, the first cause of our constitution.
For who does not know that wonder-working of nature, and [?] what the mother's womb receives, or how it transforms it? For you surely see

how simple and uniform is what is sown in the mother's bowels as the cause of the bodily existence of human beings; but what word could express the manifold variety of the composition built up from it? And if someone does not know natural science in exact detail, how could he be able to understand the diversity of that work? For indeed what is small and worthless becomes the beginning of so great and surpassing a work.

And I call it great not only with regard to the [?] of the body's structure alone, but even more because of what is worthy of wonder before this, namely the soul and the things that are observed in it.
Chapter 28.

To those who say that souls were created before bodies, or conversely that bodies were made before souls; in which the refutation of the fable of the transmigration of souls is set forth.
