And I think it is not foreign to the present subject to examine that point disputed in the churches, that is, concerning soul and body.

For the first, those who have written down fancies in books concerning first principles, say this: that an appointed city has been established for souls, and in it souls are confined as if in camps, and they have the will toward virtue and toward vice;

and that if the soul stands firm in the good, it remains without experience of union with bodies, but if it separates itself from the communion of good things, it stumbles by falling away from them and falls down into this life, and only thus are souls joined to bodies.
But others, who profess the creation of man according to the teaching of Moses, say that the soul is second in time, after the body,
since God took dust from the earth and made it into a man, and afterward made him living by his breathing.

And in this way they say that the body is more honorable than the soul, what was created first than what was breathed in; for they say that the soul was created for the sake of the body, so that what had been created might not be motionless and soulless,

and everything created for the sake of something is inferior to that for whose sake it was created, as the Gospel testifies: "The soul is more than food and the body more than clothing." For these exist for their sake; the soul does not exist for the sake of food, nor was the body created for the sake of clothing,

but those things were provided for use for the sake of the existence of these. And since the argument sets forth the grounds of this doubt on both sides, the one tells the fable of an earlier life of souls in some place set apart,

in accordance with what the fable-tellers have written, and the other is the view of those who suppose that the creation of souls came last, after the preparation of bodies. It is therefore necessary that we not pass over such questions unexamined, but undertake to set forth in argument, in exact detail on both sides, and to reveal all the improper conjectures that lie hidden in both these positions,
They call for long periods of time and many words, but we, as far as we are able, will briefly examine what has been said on both sides and then return to the matter before us.
Those who put forward the first argument and place the community life of souls ahead of the life of the body are, I think,
not free of the blasphemy of the pagans, who put forward the fable of re-embodiment.
For if anyone carefully examines their entire doctrine, he will find it armed in support of this view, on account of which they say that a certain wise man of theirs declared this, saying:
He was a man, and he put on the body of a woman, and flew up with the birds, and sprang up as a bush, and came to share in the life of water creatures.
And in my judgment, the one who speaks such nonsense about himself is, I say, not far from the truth,

for truly these blasphemies, which mix up the passing of one soul through so many bodies, are worthy of the croaking and chattering of frogs and jackdaws, the irrationality of fish, and the insensibility of oaks.

The cause of this absurdity is that they suppose the creation of souls to come before the building of the body, and this starting point of such nonsense, by bringing forth one improper argument after another, is drawn on into this kind of raving.
For if, because of some evil, the soul falls from the lofty community life, and once it has tasted bodily life, as he says,

and is made a human being again, then this much is clear: bodily life is inferior to eternal and bodiless life, and more subject to passion. And whoever falls into such a life, it is beyond doubt and dispute,
for where there are more causes of sin, one becomes associated with more evils, and becomes worse and more wicked than before. And the passion of the human soul is a likeness of the beasts.
And when it makes this its own, it is changed into the nature of the beasts, and once it has chosen evil,
it does not stop even within the bounds of the evil of beasts, for ceasing from evil becomes the beginning of a virtuous life. But among beasts there is no virtue.

And so, as it is constantly changed toward what is worse, it falls further and further into dishonor, and whatever nature it may be in, it passes over to something more evil. And just as irrational creatures are inferior to rational ones, so too the passage from irrational creatures to soulless things is a passage to something inferior.
Their argument reaches this far, then, and although it is carried along outside the truth,

yet by a certain sequence it derives one absurdity from another. But from here on, because of the incoherence of their thinking, their whole argument becomes a fable, since these subsequent accounts of theirs point to the complete destruction of the soul.

For once the soul has fallen from the lofty community life, according to their account, it can no longer stop at one measure of evil, nor is it able to, but through love of the passions it goes from being rational to being irrational,
and from irrational creatures it is changed into the nature of soulless things,
and from these it becomes entirely motionless, and after that entirely without being, and thus, by their account, the being of the soul is wholly consumed and brought to nothing,
And the return to the good becomes utterly impossible; for those who bring the soul up from a shrub or a bramble to a human being
make it plain that they present life in a bramble or a shrub as more honorable than the way of life of the bodiless.

And so, when the soul's inclination toward evil has passed over to what is lower, it will then doubtless become wholly useless, since the nature of inanimate things is lower even than that of the brute beasts, and it is to this nature that the starting point of their blasphemy brings the soul up.
But since they do not want this, either they keep the soul confined within the inanimate, or, if they bring it up from there to human life, then the shrub-like life is indeed the more honorable.

As we have said, if the fall into evil took place from that first bodiless state, and if again the ascent to virtue takes place from this present state, then this sort of blasphemy is something headless and incomplete, which presents the life of souls before the life of bodies as a life existing in its own right, and joins them to bodies because of evil.
But the second account, the one following this, is in no way less than this one in evil, the one which says that the creation of souls is later than the construction of bodies.
Therefore we reject the doctrines of both equally and hold to the middle way of orthodoxy, free from the doubts of both; that is, we neither follow the error of the pagans, who suppose
that the souls which run along with the swift revolution of heaven were weighed down by some evil and were cast down to earth,
nor again the error of those who say that the body of man was built up by a word like a statue of clay, and only afterward was the soul created for it.
For if this is so, then clay is indeed more honorable than that intelligent and bodiless nature.
Chapter 29. A demonstration that the cause of the existence of soul and body is one and the same. But,
since man is one, composed of soul and body, a common and single beginning must also be assigned to his constitution,
so that he may not be both older and younger than himself, with the bodily coming first in him and the spiritual last,
but rather, by the foreknowing divine power, in keeping with the account set forth a little earlier, one must hold and believe that the whole fullness of humanity was completed all at once,
as the prophet testifies when he says: "God knows all things beforehand, before their creation."
But in the creation of each individual it is improper to set one before the other, neither the soul before the body nor the body before the soul,

so that man may not be divided against himself and cut apart by a separation in time; for our nature is known to be twofold, according to the apostolic saying, consisting of the visible and the hidden man.

And if the one came first and the other last, then some imperfection would be attributed to the power of the Creator, as though he were not sufficient for everything in a single instant, but divided his work in two, and, parceling it out on two sides, turned to it half by half, and completed each of them separately at his leisure.

But just as we say of wheat, or of any other kind of seed, that it has gathered within itself the whole power [?] of the form of the stalk, that is, the blade and the stalk and the joints between them and the awn and the fruit,
and that, in the account of nature, none of these is before or after the existence of the seed, but rather by a certain natural order the power residing in the seed is revealed step by step,
and not that some other nature is added to it. In the same way, concerning the seed-nature of human beings, let us understand that in the first cause of the constitution of human beings, and

the power of nature is sown, and is then unfolded and revealed and brought to perfection through a certain natural sequence, not receiving any cause of perfection from outside, but bringing itself to perfection step by step.
Therefore it is not true to say either that the soul is before the body or that the body exists without the soul, but rather that one existence is to be ascribed to both:
the one, according to the exalted divine will, constituted together in the first creation; and the second, united in the cause of human existence;

for just as the articulation of the limbs is not seen in the cause of the body's existence before conception, so too the properties of the soul cannot be perceived in it before they are shown forth in action,

and just as no one doubts that this cause of existence is shaped into the various kinds of limbs and inner organs, not because some other power is added to it, but because the power residing within it by nature becomes what makes it grow.
In the same way one must understand concerning the soul
that, even though it is not recognized from any visible acts, it is in no way lacking from it.
For the form of the human being who is to be constructed is present in it in potency, but it is unknown and hidden, because it cannot be manifested before the necessary sequence.
So too the soul is present in it, even though it is not visible, but it becomes visible through its own natural movement and activity, growing along with the growth of the body.
For since the power of conception is not separated off from mortal bodies,

but from ensouled and living ones, for this reason we say that it is right that no one should suppose that the existence brought forth from a living being as the cause of a living being is mortal and soulless,
for in bodies what is soulless is without doubt also dead. And deadness comes about through the privation of the soul.

And no one can say that privation comes before the entry into existence, or that it is older than the constitution, nor can anyone say that the soulless, which is deadness and alien to the soul, takes precedence over the soul.
But if someone should seek a clearer sign on this point, and concerning that which becomes the beginning of the living being that is to be born,
it is possible to understand this also from other indications, by which the ensouled is distinguished from the dead,
for the sign of human life is this: that a person be warm and strong and moving.
But what is cold and motionless in bodies is nothing other than deadness.
Now therefore, since we see in what is warm and moving and living that cause of existence of which we are speaking, it is clear that it is not soulless either.

And just as, with regard to its bodily nature, we do not call it flesh and bone and hair and all the members that are seen in human beings, although in potency it is the cause of all these, yet it has not yet been visibly brought forth;
so also with regard to the spiritual part we say that it does not yet have a place capable of containing those parts of the soul, namely reason and desire and anger and the others that follow them.
But in correspondence with the completion and growth of the body, the powers of the soul also grow together with that which lies beneath it.
For just as, when a person has become mature, the power and activity of the soul become evident through higher deeds,

so also at the beginning of existence, in measure and in correspondence with that time, the power of the soul likewise makes itself known, and from the sown matter it prepares it as a dwelling for itself, skillfully and wonderfully.

For it is not possible for the soul to settle in buildings foreign to it, just as the impression in wax does not fit a foreign seal; but just as the body is brought up to maturity from that contemptible origin,
so also the power of the soul, in correspondence with the shoot, spreads out and is revealed together with that growth,
for in that first preparation it goes before it, like some root planted in the earth, with only the power of sprouting and growth,
for that smallness cannot contain anything more. And afterward, when the plant has come out into the light, it spreads out its shoot under the sun, and this shoot is the blossoming of sensation.
And when it has grown strong and risen to its height, then, like fruit, the power of speech begins to shine forth; yet it does not all appear at once,
but it increases along with the completion of the organ and through the labor of growth, and it always becomes only as fruitful as the power of that plant can contain.
But if you seek the powers and works of the soul within the structure of the body, examine yourself, as Moses says, and read the account of the soul's works as if in a book,

for nature itself will tell you, more clearly than any word, of the soul's skills and occupations in the various parts of the body, both individually and all together, on account of those structures of its
which it prepares. I consider it superfluous to set these forth, as though I were to declare one's own affairs as if they belonged to someone else. For who would there be
who looks at himself and would need instruction about his own nature? For whoever examines the pattern of this life

and understands how the body is suited to all the activities of living can know to what purpose the power of the soul devoted itself, the power able to make the plant of the body, fashioned from the beginning, grow. And if anyone is not without understanding, it is clear from this too
that what the furnace of nature received was neither dead nor soulless, that which was cut from living bodies and planted as the seedling of a living being,

for we plant in the earth the heart of trees and the shoot of roots, not as things dead to the natural power that is in them, but as things that secretly preserve within themselves the character of their firstborn plants [?].

And the earth does not breathe such power into them from outside somehow, for if this were so, it would be able to make even rotten wood and dead trees sprout and grow green. Rather, it brings out and makes manifest the power that is within them, enriched by its own moisture,
and through roots and branches and heart and bark it makes the plant grow to its completion,

which it could not do unless some natural power were joined to it, one that drew to itself, from the neighbouring earth and moisture, the nourishment that is its own, kindred and similar to it, and by itself changed, reaching completion as a shrub, or a tree, or a stalk [?], or other herbs and green plants.
Chapter 30. A medical examination of the constitution of our body. Briefly, then, in this way each person's own nature teaches and instructs him in detail about the constitution of our body,

from which it is formed and is seen and lives and perceives. But each person should also investigate and learn in detail about this subject from the accounts written down in books with much labor by the wise,

some of whom learned from cutting open and examining the entrails how each of our inner members is arranged, and others considered for what purpose all the members of our body were created, or what their united assistance to one another is,
and they studied their joining together and related it to us, so that lovers of learning may learn from this a sufficient understanding of the human constitution.
But if anyone seeks to have the Church become his teacher of all things,

and to have no need of any outside voice — for this is the law of the spiritual sheep, as the Lord says: "They will not listen to the voice of a stranger" — let us set forth a brief and abridged account on this subject too:
We understand, then, that there are three natures of the body, through which our whole being is constituted within us, each part individually:
one so that we may live, another so that we may live well, and the other has its constitution for the preservation of successive continuance.
And all those things in us without which human life is impossible, we understand to lie in three parts, which are the head, the heart and the liver.
And all the increase of good things, the honor of nature and the living well that are bestowed on a person through them
are established in the organs of the senses, which do not bestow life on us, for often some of them are lacking in a person,
and he goes on living just the same, but without their help it is impossible to share in the sweetness of the delights of this life.
And again, the third aspect looks toward successive continuance.

And there are also certain others besides these, which together stand ready as maintainers of the existence of all, and which through themselves bring in the suitable additions, such as the lung and the belly, of which the one kindles the fire of the heart and the other supplies nourishment to the entrails.
Thus, then, from the division of our constitution it is clearly understood that the power of our life is not governed in a single way, or by any one thing,
but nature has distributed the causes and sustainers of our constitution among many parts and members, and makes the help of each one necessary to all the others.
Hence, whatever nature has skillfully devised as a guard of life and as an adornment of beauty, such things are many and differ greatly from one another.
But I think that I should first briefly distinguish those first principles and sustainers of our life.

Now let the materials of the whole body, which are common to our members, be passed over in silence for the present, for natural philosophy about all of them does not contribute to this kind of inquiry, which we are undertaking in order to examine particular matters. It is acknowledged by all, then,
that parts of all the elements of the world are seen in us,
that is, of the hot and the cold, of the moist and the dry, and we have with us the [?] of them all.

Hence we see three powers that sustain life. One of them warms everything with heat, while the second moistens with moisture what has been heated, so that by the balancing of those opposing qualities [?] it may keep the living creature in the mean, so that neither the moisture dries up through an excess of heat, nor the heat is extinguished through an excess of moisture.
The third power by itself makes firm and joins together the separated parts, and blends and governs them,
and extends to them all the self-moving and choosing power; if this is lacking, the body is dissolved and dies. This is the governing and choosing soul.

Hence we must diligently examine the skill of our nature, in nature itself, concerning the constitution of the flesh. For since what is hard and resistant does not admit the activity of the senses, as is seen in us in the bones, and in the earth in plants and trees,

in which we see a certain form of life through nourishment and growth, yet their resistance and hardness did not admit the power of sensation, it was therefore necessary that before the activity of the senses there should be set a certain wax-like constitution, to receive the imprint of those powers that are the helpers of the one who observes,

neither confusing the seal by excessive softness, for what is impressed on the moist and wet does not remain, nor resisting by immoderate hardening, so that it should not be unyielding and incapable of being shaped,

for what is firm and hard cannot be shaped; but it is set at the mean between hardness and softness, so that man should not be left without a share in those good powers of nature, which is movement through the senses.
But since what is tender and soft, if it has no help from anything hard and firm, becomes immobile, shapeless and unjointed, like the soft creatures of the sea,

therefore nature mixed the firmness of the bones with the softness of the flesh, and joined and combined these with one another in a beautiful union, and strengthened their joints with the bond of the sinews, and only then made the flesh that receives the senses grow upon them,
And he stretched over them the firmer and stronger substance of the skin,
and upon the solid nature of the bones, as upon weight-bearing pillars, he loaded this whole burden of flesh; and he did not set up those pillars of bone in the body without joints,
for if it were so, the human frame would be immobile and useless, and like a tree it would stand in one place,
and neither would the alternation of the feet direct its walking toward the paths lying before it, nor would the service of the hands be fit for the necessary uses of life. But as it is,

he has made that instrument of the body ready both to walk and to act, by the contrivance of the joints and by the governing and self-ruling soul; and these, through the fastening of the sinews, established the power of movement and impulse in the flesh by means of the bowels [?] and the joints.
And then there is the service of the hands, varied and of many forms, adapted and fit for every contrivance,
and the turning of the neck, and the bending and raising of the head, and the movement and action of the chin [?],

and the narrowing, opening and shutting of the eyelids, performed with intelligence, and the movement of the other joints, which are carried out like some kind of machines by the drawing up and slackening of the sinews,
while the power proceeding from them has a certain self-commanded impulse, through the soul that decides what is fitting and through a certain governance of nature,

brought to completion in each of the members. And as the root and origin of the movement of all the sinews we name the sinews that enclose the head, and the membranes and skins of the brain. And, as I think, there is no further need for a precise inquiry about the life-generating members, of what kind they are and how they are, since here we have shown the working of their motion, which the sinews of the neck perform.
But only this: that the head has great power for life, and this is made plain
if anything adverse befalls it, that is, a severe wound or a tearing of the membranes of the brain, for death too follows immediately upon that injury.

For indeed nature cannot endure such a wound even for a moment; just as when a foundation is shaken the whole building is destroyed together with that part. And when by its injury every living creature perishes, who would not acknowledge that the causes of its life truly reside in it?
And since the living creature has ceased from life, the natural heat also is quenched and the dead body grows cold.

For this reason we said that the cause of vitality is also seen in heat; for when a thing is such that death follows upon its lack, it must be acknowledged that its coming is what provides life to the living creature.

And we understand the heart to be the source and origin of such a power, from which go out the manifold courts [?] of the heart, like 'nectars' [?] and channels, and they are sown, each in a different direction, throughout the whole body and spread abroad the hot and fire-like spirit. And since some nourishment and matter was needed for that heat, nature surely did not leave that lacking either,
for fire cannot persist by itself without matter, unless it is nourished and kept in motion in a manner suited to its own constitution.
For this reason also streams of blood come out from the liver, as from a spring, and, heated by that boiling spirit, travel about through the whole body and circulate,
so that they may not be isolated from one another, become a disease, and destroy the nature. Let this teach the disorderly about equity,

and let them learn from nature that greed is an evil passion, destructive and rapacious. But since God alone is without lack, while human poverty, in order to sustain its constitution, is in need of external necessities, therefore by these three powers

of which we have spoken the whole body is governed. For through various paths and entrances, like a river, it takes in matter from outside, and it distributes it suitably to each part and stores it up.
For the spring of blood,

which is the liver, stores it up by receiving food, for the foods continually entering through it make the liver produce rivers of blood, just as snow lying on a mountain multiplies the springs at the foot of the mountain by its moisture, for it lets its moisture down into the depths of the earth, as through veins, and makes the eye of the spring swell.

And the flame or breeze of the heart is brought in from the neighboring organ and member called the lung, which is a storehouse of air. Through the joints of its structure the lung reaches up to the mouth and the palate, and, like a kind of pipe,
it breathes in the air from outside and by this breathing draws it inward,
into the midst of which the heart is fixed. And like the power of that ever-moving fire, this too moves continually.

And just as bellows do in smithies, so this draws to itself from the breath nearby, fills the courts and channels of the heart with that breeze, kindles its flame, and spreads it to the neighboring members and organs. And it gives this no respite at all, for by drawing in from outside through breathing it fills its channels, and by emptying inward it sends it on to the members. And, as I suppose,
this too is the cause of our breathing of its own accord, for often our mind is occupied with other matters,
or even falls entirely silent when the body is released by sleep, yet the breathing of the air does not cease or diminish, even though it has no help at all in this matter from the will.
For since the heart is surrounded by the lung, and the lung occupies the part behind the heart,
and by its swelling [?] and closing it moves the organs, the breathing in and breathing out of the air is appointed as the work of the lung,
for it is thin and spacious, and keeps all its cavities inflated and raised up in the depths of the windpipe [?], like a pipe.
And when it contracts and the air goes out of it, the breath remaining in its pipes and cavities is forcibly driven out and escapes.
And when it has gone out and the lung has opened, by that opening it draws in the air again and fills what was emptied.
And this is the cause of this involuntary breathing: the unceasing motion of air and fire.

And since motion is proper to heat, and we have found the source of this heat in the heart, the heart by its perpetual motion brings about the unceasing inhalation and exhalation of air through the lung.

Hence, if the fierceness of the heat should increase beyond what is natural through the inflammation of illness, both exhalation and inhalation increase all the more, as though the heart were hastening, because of the heat within it, to quench it with a fresher breeze.
For since our nature is poor and procures from every side what sustains its own constitution, it is not only in need of breeze and air,

to kindle the heat, which it continually procures from outside and cherishes for the life of the living being, but food too, that which strengthens the body, is likewise procured by it through contrivance.

Hence by eating and drinking it fills up its deficiency; for it implanted in the bodily frame a power that draws in what is lacking and disperses what is in excess, and by this it gives no small help to nature,
so that it may kindle and feed that fire of the heart. For since one of the chief and vital members,
as we said above, is the heart, which by that hot breath gives life to each of the parts of the body,

our Creator so fashioned it that with its vigorous power it might govern mightily on every side, so that none of its parts should remain idle and useless, entirely without its governance. For this reason nature also placed the lung behind it, on account of its perpetual motion,
the lung, which draws the air toward itself, and when it draws it in, it expands its inner passages; but when it breathes out, it contracts again and sends forth again the breath it has held in.

And in front of it, it fashioned the mouth of the upper belly and made it hot, and it stirs it to its own tasks and makes it labor, compelling it not to draw in breath but to receive foods of every kind.
For the passages of the lung and of the stomach are somewhat close to one another,
and they go up side by side like twins, and extend, and end evenly in the mouth; and the one becomes the entrance and door for food, and the other for breath.
However, in the depth the gullet and the windpipe no longer remain joined,
for the heart places itself between the two, and to the one it imparts the power of exhalation, and to the other the power of food.
For the nature of fire seeks material to burn, and this necessarily comes upon the storehouse of food,
for the more it is heated by that neighboring heat, the more it draws in the material of heat.

And this kind of inclination we call the appetite for eating. And when that fire of the heart finds the material of food, that which sustains nature, and rises up against it, even then it does not rest, but, as in a furnace, it melts those materials.

And when it has melted them and thinned them, it makes them flow, as through a kind of funnel or pipe, toward those other channels and ducts. And when it has separated the thick from the pure, it directs the fine and pure part through certain conduits to the gates of the liver,

But the material, coarse and heavy part of the food it weighs out and sends on to the broad intestines, turns it about in their many-coiled windings, and holds the food back so that it lingers in the intestines,

so that it may not, through the straightness of the passage, easily pour out and at once stir the living creature to desire for food, and so that man may not thus be without any rest from eating, like the nature of the beasts.
But since the liver above all needed the help of heat to change the moist juices into blood, and yet by its position it is set apart from the heart (for, as I think, it was not even possible,

since it is the root and beginning of the vital power, that its dominion should be hemmed in by a second ruling principle), and so that its ordering might suffer no harm through this separation from the heat,
for this reason, through the vessels that are called arteries, it receives from the heart that hot breath; and the liver takes in the streams that are sent to it and makes them boil with that heat,
and changes them to the color of blood, according to the property of fire,
and makes them crimson. And then from there they are divided, like twin streams mingled together,

and each has its own power within itself, that is, breath and blood, so that they may be apt for traveling, for the moisture is made light by the heat. And thus they spread through the whole body in many ways and are changed into myriad channels and nectar [?] of various kinds.

And when these two principles of the vital powers have joined with one another, they spread heat and moisture to every part of the body, and, as a kind of necessary bond, they carry themselves up toward the most principal power that governs our life, which is seen in the head and brain and in the nerves and joints of the head and neck,
from which come all the movement of the ligaments and joints, and all the strength of the composite parts, and all the governance of the soul,
sown in each of the limbs, which, as if by some machine, show this earthen statue of ours to be moving and active.

For the purity of the heat and the fineness of the moisture, united and joined by the twin powers, nourish and sustain the head by means of vapors; and again, from there a still purer and finer vapor nourishes and feeds the membranes of the brain and the skin of the head,

which is spread over the top and goes down into the depth like a pipe and like a channel, and descends in succession through the ligaments of the neck, and encloses the head itself and the brain within it, and comes to its end at the beginning of the feet. And by the composition of all the bones and ligaments and by the structure of the flesh and joints,
like some charioteer, so the head gives each part its movement and position and direction and power,
for which reason it has also received a firmer enclosure, for it is surrounded by the joining of two bones,
and it is made firm by the many-stranded composition of the sinews of the neck and by bones and ligaments, so that it remains unharmed through the care of nature.
And the same is to be understood concerning the heart, for, like some walled house, so its dwelling is enclosed,
For at the back the spine and the area between the shoulder blades protect it, and on this side and that the ribs strengthen it,

while in front the chest encloses it, and thus it remains untouched by external things that could harm it. And, to speak briefly, just as the work of husbandry and the planting of gardens and orchards is seen, so also understand the human constitution, as if some garden or orchard lay before you, irrigated by water or by rain,
filled with saplings and countless plants and fruits of the earth, whose form, richness, and coloring were seen to be distinct and diverse in each one,
and though these are so many, the water that nourishes them is one in nature, while the things nourished differ, each in its own form and in many kinds.
And see how that one water thus transforms itself into many forms: for the same water turns bitter in wormwood, and in hemlock becomes destructive,
and it becomes different again in saffron, balsam, and poppy, for in one it grows hot, in another it grows cold, and in another it becomes balanced in its richness.
And in the laurel, the mastic, and others of this kind it becomes fragrant, and in the fig and the pear it grows sweet, and in the vine it is changed into grape and wine,
and the tastiness of the apple, the color of the pomegranate, the crimson of the rose, the brilliance of the lily, the violet hue of the violet, and the sky-blue of the hyacinth,

and everything, however much is seen upon the earth, all springs up from one and the same water. And these things, so many and of such kinds, so variously distinguished in form, kind, and richness, grow in one soil and one orchard by one moisture.
Such wonder-working is also seen accomplished by nature in that animate orchard and garden of ours, or rather by the King of natures: bones and cartilage and veins and arteries and sinews
and ligaments and flesh and skin and marrow and fats and hair and fingers and nails and eyes and nostrils and ears,
and all these and countless others of the kind, distinguished from one another by their various properties,
are nourished by nature from one food, and when the body receives the food into the diversity of all its members, it makes its power proper to each member.
That is, to the eyes it gives sight, and to the eyelids fineness and separation,
to the ears hearing, to the lips movement, and to the tongue its turning about; for among the bones it hardens, in the marrow it softens, and in the sinews it grows firm,
and it spreads over the skin and the face, and it is changed into nail and hair.

And if it carries winding vapors up to the head through crooked and twisted pores, it grows curly and twisted hair. But if those vapors that produce the hair rise straight and direct, they bring forth reed-straight, smooth hair. However, as I think,
our discourse has strayed far from the path set before it, for I am investigating and enumerating the works of nature and undertaking to describe them,

And how, or from what source, each part of our constitution was prepared — how much of it is suited for living, how much for living well, and whatever else there is along with these — we have understood according to the division stated above.
For the proposed aim of this discourse of ours was this: to show the cause of our generation from seed,
and that neither is the soul without a body, nor the body without a soul, but that from ensouled and living bodies an ensouled, living creature is born from the very beginning,

which human nature receives, like a kind of nurse, and fattens by its own powers; and it is nourished on both sides, and its growth becomes perceptible and manifest in a manner corresponding to each of the two parts.
For immediately, through that powerful and skilful creation, the power of the soul that is blended with it appears, at first brought forth invisibly and in a hidden way,
but afterward shining forth with the completion of the organ, just as can be seen with stonecutters,

who have set before them the aim of sculpting in stone the form of some living creature. The one who undertakes to complete it in practice first cuts the stone out from the rocks joined to it, and then cuts away the surplus material and gives it the general shape of the form he intends, according to his will,
until even an ignorant person may recognize the craftsman's intent and what form he means to produce. And as he adds further labor, he draws closer to the likeness for which he was striving.
And then he carves the complete and true form on the material and thus brings his craft to completion, and the sculpted thing is a lion or a man, or whatever the craftsman's will has decided upon,
which was previously unmarked and formless, a mere stone. Yet the material was not changed into the form; rather, the form was imprinted on the material.
And if anyone understands the same pattern with regard to the soul, he will not stray from the truth, for we say that:
the all-skilful nature receives that part of man within itself, most wonderfully transforms it, and fashions it into a rational statue.

And just as the form was joined to the material of the stone little by little through labor — at first more dimly and more faintly, but after the completion of the work more clearly and more brilliantly — so too, in the sculpting of this human organ, the form of the soul appears in correspondence with the material underlying it: incompletely in the incomplete, and completely in the complete.

And if nature had not been corrupted through evil, it would have been complete from the beginning. For this reason, its sharing in that passible and brutish birth does not allow the divine image to shine forth immediately in what is formed,
but by a certain movement and progress and sequence, through the material and brutish properties of the soul, it brings man up to completion.
And the great Apostle also sets forth this teaching to the Corinthians, saying: "When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I reasoned as a child, I was accounted as a child.

"But when I became a man, I put away the things of childhood." This does not mean that another soul enters into the man, apart from the soul that was seen in the child, which leaves behind the mind of childhood and takes on that of manhood. Rather, that same soul is imperfect at that stage of life,
but in this second stage it shows perfection. And just as we speak of life in the case of a plant and of whatever grows,
and no one counts as soulless anything that by nature moves and shares in life, yet neither will anyone say that such a life is receptive of a perfect soul,
for when the activity of the soul enters into plants, it cannot rise as far as sense perception.

And again, when a higher power of the soul is spread over the irrational animals, that too is not perfect, since it cannot contain within itself the grace of reason and mind. For this reason we say that:
The true and perfect soul is the human soul alone, perfected by all the powers of mind and speech.
As for anything else that shares in life, people by common custom reckon it as animate, although there is no perfect soul in such things, but only some part of the power of soul,
which, as we have learned from the teaching of Moses in the mystery of the creation of man, is present in man as well, on account of the passibility that he made his own.
For this reason Paul counsels those under his obedience to attain perfection, and he also teaches them the way in which they may reach it, saying to them:
"Strip off the old man and put on the renewed one, according to the image of his Creator."
But let us go back up once more to that God-clothed grace with which God adorned man in the beginning, when he said:
"Let us make man in our image and likeness." To him be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.
